question_text: What is Phase 1 and Phase 2 debris removal, and what do I need to do?
official_question: What is Phase 1 and Phase 2 debris removal, and what do I need to do?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner whose home was destroyed or severely damaged by the Eaton Fire wants to understand the government-managed debris removal process and what choices they need to make.

source_answer.official_answer: Private property debris removal after the Eaton Fire proceeds in two distinct phases managed by different federal agencies. Phase 1 is managed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA): EPA-certified field teams inspect properties and safely remove and dispose of household hazardous materials — including visible asbestos-containing items, batteries, solvents, pesticides, and other household hazardous waste — at no cost to the property owner. Properties must receive EPA Phase 1 clearance before moving to Phase 2. Phase 2 is fire debris removal — everything remaining after Phase 1 clearance, including fire ash, soil, metals, hazardous trees, and foundation debris. After Phase 1 clearance, property owners must choose one of two options: (1) Opt in to cleanup by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers at no cost to the homeowner; or (2) Opt out and hire an approved private contractor to remove all remaining fire debris following all applicable safety rules and regulations. You should not attempt to remove or store ash and debris from a destroyed or severely damaged property on your own, as improper handling can release toxic chemicals, fibers, or particles into the air. Track Phase 1 progress using the EPA Status Map at storymaps.arcgis.com.

question_text: My home had solar panels and a home battery. What do I do with them after the fire?
official_question: My home had solar panels and a home battery. What do I do with them after the fire?
normalized_resident_need: A resident with a home battery system, solar panels, or electric vehicle on a fire-damaged property wants to know how to handle damaged lithium-ion batteries safely.

source_answer.official_answer: Fire-damaged or destroyed lithium-ion batteries — including home energy storage systems, solar battery backup units, and batteries in electric or hybrid vehicles — are extremely dangerous and should not be touched or disturbed. Even if they appear intact, damaged lithium-ion batteries can spontaneously re-ignite, explode, and emit toxic gases and particulates. Do not touch fire-damaged products with lithium-ion batteries — they can ignite. Do not start, move, tow, or charge a fire-damaged electric or hybrid vehicle. Do not use or start a fire-damaged residential energy storage or house battery. Do not enter enclosed spaces containing lithium-ion battery products. Call the U.S. EPA hotline at 1-833-R9-USEPA (1-833-798-7372) if you encounter a lithium-ion battery while re-entering your property or if you are unsure whether a battery was damaged. The EPA has been assigned by FEMA to remove lithium-ion batteries affected by the Los Angeles County wildfires as part of Phase 1 debris removal.
required_answer_elements: State that fire-damaged lithium-ion batteries are extremely dangerous and can re-ignite, explode, or emit toxic gases even if they appear intact.
Tell the user NOT to touch, move, start, or charge any fire-damaged lithium-ion battery product.
Provide the EPA hotline 1-833-798-7372 for reporting or asking about damaged batteries.
Explain that the EPA handles lithium-ion battery removal as part of Phase 1 debris removal.
forbidden_claims: Telling the user it is safe to move or transport a fire-damaged battery if it looks undamaged.
Suggesting the user can handle or dispose of a damaged battery themselves.
Inventing different EPA hotline numbers.
Stating that only EV batteries are dangerous (home storage systems are equally hazardous).

question_text: My pool and spa weren't burned but they're full of ash and soot. Is it safe to use them, and what should I do?
official_question: My pool and spa weren't burned but they're full of ash and soot. Is it safe to use them, and what should I do?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose pool or spa was not destroyed but was exposed to wildfire ash and soot wants to know whether it is safe to use and how to get it back in service.

source_answer.official_answer: Do not use a pool or spa that has been exposed to wildfire smoke, soot, or ash until you have completed the cleanup steps outlined in the LA County Department of Public Health Swimming Pools After a Fire guidance. Even if the pool structure is undamaged, ash and soot can introduce harmful contaminants into the water. If your pool or spa enclosure was damaged or destroyed by the fire, the U.S. EPA or U.S. Army Corps may install a temporary enclosure to protect workers during Phase 1 and Phase 2 of Private Property Debris Removal. If your pool or spa structure was damaged or destroyed, follow the steps in the LACDPH Swimming Pools After a Fire guidance once your property is cleared for rebuilding, and use licensed professional services for inspection and repairs to ensure compliance with local codes before reopening. For questions, contact the LA County Environmental Health Recreational Waters Program at (626) 430-5360 or email rhealth@ph.lacounty.gov.
required_answer_elements: State clearly that the pool or spa should NOT be used until cleanup steps are completed.
Direct the user to the LA County Department of Public Health Swimming Pools resources.
Provide the LA County Environmental Health Recreational Waters Program contact: (626) 430-5360 or rhealth@ph.lacounty.gov.
forbidden_claims: Telling the user the pool is safe to use as long as it looks clean.
Providing specific pool chemistry or chlorination instructions not in the source.
Guaranteeing that any specific cleaning method will make the pool safe.
Telling the user damaged pool structures can be repaired without a permit or professional inspection.

question_text: Is it safe to eat vegetables and fruit from my garden after the fire? What about my soil?
official_question: Is it safe to eat vegetables and fruit from my garden after the fire? What about my soil?
normalized_resident_need: A resident with a home garden in the Eaton Fire area wants to know whether their produce and soil are safe to use and how to handle them.

source_answer.official_answer: Wildfire ash and soot can settle on soil, plants, and produce and may contain harmful contaminants including heavy metals and chemicals. For home produce: check for visible ash on topsoil, plants, and trees. Wearing protective gear, pre-rinse produce outside with a hose or bucket of clean water to remove soil and ash. Wash hands before handling produce indoors. Remove outer leaves of lettuce or leafy greens. Rinse and rub produce under cool running water; peel before cooking or serving. Soak deeply veined greens like kale, and fuzzy fruits like peaches, in a 10% white vinegar solution to remove soil particles. Avoid root crops like carrots or potatoes that grow in the soil, as they absorb more contaminants. Avoid planting crops in contaminated soil. For soil safety, LA County Public Health recommends testing soils in urban gardens — especially near burned areas — using a lab heavy metals panel (lead, cadmium, arsenic, nickel, mercury). Do not use ash as fertilizer, as it may contain harmful residues. Consult the LACDPH Guidance on Eating Produce from a Home Garden and UC Cooperative Extension's Produce Safety After Urban Wildfire for detailed guidance.
required_answer_elements: Advise washing produce thoroughly and removing outer leaves before eating.
Warn against eating root vegetables (like carrots or potatoes) grown in potentially contaminated soil.
Recommend soil testing for heavy metals, especially near burned structures.
Advise against using ash as fertilizer.
forbidden_claims: Telling the user all home produce is safe to eat without any precautions.
Inventing specific contamination levels or safe thresholds.
Recommending specific lab vendors.
Promising any washing method eliminates all contamination risk.
Stating that fruit from trees is always unsafe (properly washed fruit from trees is generally considered safe per guidance).

question_text: How do I keep my pets safe with all the ash and bad air quality?
official_question: How do I keep my pets safe with all the ash and bad air quality?
normalized_resident_need: A resident wants to know how to protect their pets from wildfire ash, soot, and poor air quality following the Eaton Fire.

source_answer.official_answer: Pets face similar health risks from wildfire ash and poor air quality as humans, and in some cases may be more vulnerable because they are lower to the ground and may ingest ash by licking their paws or fur. Keep pets indoors as much as possible, especially during periods of poor air quality or active debris removal nearby. Use air purifiers with HEPA filters to improve indoor air quality where pets spend time. Avoid walking pets in ash-covered areas; if they must go outside, clean their paws with a damp cloth after outdoor exposure and consider wiping their fur as well. Provide pets with fresh, clean water at all times and avoid letting them drink from standing water in fire-affected areas. Children, pregnant individuals, and pets should avoid areas until hazards are fully mitigated. If your pet shows signs of respiratory distress — coughing, wheezing, labored breathing, or excessive lethargy — contact a veterinarian.

question_text: I own a small business and the fire damaged my building and equipment. Where can I get help?
official_question: I own a small business and the fire damaged my building and equipment. Where can I get help?
normalized_resident_need: A business owner affected by the Eaton Fire wants to know whether SBA disaster loans are available to businesses and how to apply.

source_answer.official_answer: The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) offers low-interest disaster loans to businesses of all sizes, private nonprofit organizations, homeowners, and renters affected by the Eaton Fire. Businesses can apply for up to $2 million to repair or replace damaged real estate, machinery, equipment, inventory, and other business assets. The interest rate for small businesses is 4% with terms up to 30 years. SBA also encourages applicants to apply even if they are not sure they need the loan, because the application establishes eligibility for other SBA programs. Apply online at lending.sba.gov, call 1-800-659-2955 (TTY 1-800-877-8339), or visit an SBA Disaster Loan Outreach Center in person — one is located at Pasadena City College Community Education Center, 3035 E. Foothill Blvd., Pasadena. The deadline to apply for the Eaton Fire is March 31, 2025. SBA does not charge a fee to apply.

question_text: My car is covered in ash from the fire. How do I safely clean it?
official_question: My car is covered in ash from the fire. How do I safely clean it?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose vehicle was exposed to wildfire ash and soot wants to know how to clean it safely without damaging the paint or exposing themselves to hazardous particles.

source_answer.official_answer: Ash and soot from wildfire debris can be abrasive and may contain hazardous particles. Wear gloves and an N95 or P-100 respirator while cleaning your vehicle outdoors. Start by gently rinsing the vehicle with a hose to remove loose ash before scrubbing — do not dry-scrub ash, as it can scratch the paint and stir particles into the air. Use a mild detergent and water to clean exterior surfaces, then rinse thoroughly. Check all air intake vents and filters and remove any accumulated debris. If ash has entered the vehicle interior, use a HEPA-filter vacuum to clean carpets, seats, and surfaces, then wipe down hard surfaces with a damp cloth. Change the cabin air filter if the vehicle has one, as it may have captured ash and soot particles during the event. Wash your hands and change clothes after cleaning to avoid tracking contaminants indoors.

question_text: My house wasn't burned, but ash from nearby properties makes it unsafe to live in. Will my insurance still cover my temporary living costs?
official_question: My house wasn't burned, but ash from nearby properties makes it unsafe to live in. Will my insurance still cover my temporary living costs?
normalized_resident_need: A homeowner or renter whose property was not directly burned by the Eaton Fire but is uninhabitable due to nearby ash, debris, or public health advisory conditions wants to know whether their ALE insurance coverage continues.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes. Per California Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara's February 14, 2025 Notice on Additional Living Expense (ALE) Coverage, if your home has been impacted by the 2025 Southern California wildfires (including the Palisades and Eaton fires) and is deemed uninhabitable due to health and safety reasons — such as hazardous fire debris or ash from nearby properties — your insurance company is expected to continue providing Additional Living Expenses (ALE) coverage, also known as Loss of Use or Fair Rental Value coverage. This applies even if utilities like water and power have been restored to your address. Insurance companies must exercise due diligence in determining whether a home is habitable or uninhabitable. ALE coverage applies for policyholders in affected areas until their homes are deemed habitable, subject to applicable statutory timeframes and any policy limits that may apply, as long as the County's Public Health Advisory remains in effect. Contact your insurance company or adjuster directly with questions, or reach the California Department of Insurance at their consumer hotline at (800) 927-4357 or online at www.insurance.ca.gov.

question_text: My clothes and bedding smell like smoke from the fire. How do I clean them safely?
official_question: My clothes and bedding smell like smoke from the fire. How do I clean them safely?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose clothing, bedding, or other fabric items were exposed to wildfire smoke and ash wants to know how to safely clean them.

source_answer.official_answer: Clothing, bedding, and other fabric items exposed to wildfire smoke and ash can contain harmful particles. Before washing, shake out visible soot outdoors while wearing protective gear (gloves, N95 respirator, long sleeves) and away from the home to avoid bringing particles inside. Wash items in small loads using regular laundry detergent. Some suggest adding a cup of white vinegar or another deodorizer to help neutralize smoke odors. Repeat the washing cycle if smoke smell persists. Do not use the dryer until all smoke odors are removed, as heat can permanently set smoke smell into fabric. Depending on the extent of smoke damage inside your washer or dryer, consider cleaning the appliances or having them professionally serviced before use, to avoid re-contaminating clean items. Items with heavy smoke damage or delicate fabrics may benefit from professional cleaning services.

question_text: What dangerous substances are in the ash and debris from the fire? Should I be worried about asbestos or lead?
official_question: What dangerous substances are in the ash and debris from the fire? Should I be worried about asbestos or lead?
normalized_resident_need: A resident wants to understand what dangerous substances may be present in wildfire ash and debris, specifically whether asbestos and lead are a concern, and what to do about it.

source_answer.official_answer: Fire debris from damaged and destroyed homes can contain many harmful substances. These may include asbestos from older building materials (especially in homes built before the 1980s), toxic heavy metals such as lead, mercury, arsenic, and cadmium, dangerous chemicals from household products such as pesticides and solvents, and harmful particles and compounds created by combustion itself — including dioxins, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Asbestos is a particular concern in older construction; if your home was built before the 1980s, ceiling materials such as popcorn ceilings may contain asbestos. Do not disturb or attempt to clean materials you suspect contain asbestos, as doing so can release harmful fibers into the air. Residents can hire certified professionals — including environmental consultants, certified industrial hygienists (CIH), asbestos inspectors, and lead risk assessors — to conduct testing and cleanup. The LA County Department of Public Health does not provide testing or recommend specific companies. During Phase 1 of Private Property Debris Removal, the U.S. EPA removes visible hazardous materials, including identifiable asbestos-containing items, from fire-damaged properties at no cost to the owner.

question_text: My house wasn't burned but I think there might be smoke damage inside. How do I check?
official_question: My house wasn't burned but I think there might be smoke damage inside. How do I check?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose home was not burned but may have sustained smoke damage wants to know how to evaluate the extent of damage before starting cleanup or filing an insurance claim.

source_answer.official_answer: Before entering, wear protective gear: N95 or P-100 respirator, goggles, gloves, long sleeves, long pants, and closed-toe shoes. Walk the exterior and look for obvious signs of fire and smoke damage, checking for ash or soot buildup on siding, doors, and windows. Photograph and document all findings for your insurance carrier before undertaking any remediation or cleanup. Walk the interior room by room and assess the extent of smoke, soot, and ash contamination, including in air vents. If there is a noticeable smoke odor, you likely have some level of smoke damage. In cases where there is no visible soot, a wipe test — wiping a wall or windowsill with a white cloth — can help determine whether ash or soot is present. For situations with light soot on horizontal surfaces, airborne particulate, or noticeable smoke odors, a more thorough cleaning is recommended. Do not turn on your HVAC system until the bulk of the soot and ash has been cleaned up: running the system beforehand will spread particulate and re-contaminate surfaces that have already been cleaned. If you are filing an insurance claim, the insurer may send a field adjuster and may have firms they recommend or contract with for assessment and restoration work.

question_text: How do I find a reputable company to clean up smoke damage in my home?
official_question: How do I find a reputable company to clean up smoke damage in my home?
normalized_resident_need: A resident needs to hire a professional cleaning or restoration contractor for smoke and ash damage and wants to know how to find a qualified, legitimate one and avoid scams.

source_answer.official_answer: When selecting a professional cleaning or restoration contractor for smoke, soot, and ash restoration, take the following steps. First, if you are filing an insurance claim, check with your insurance company — they may have firms they recommend or contract with for this type of work. If you are finding a contractor yourself: verify the contractor is properly licensed by the State or County and has required bonding and liability insurance. Check with the Better Business Bureau (bbb.org) and ask for and follow up with references. Request certifications from organizations like the Institute of Inspection Cleaning and Restoration Certification (IICRC) at iicrc.org and the Restoration Industry Association (RIA) at restorationindustry.org. Before any work begins, obtain a detailed written estimate including the scope of work and schedule — do not proceed without one. Understand all contract terms, including what is required of you (such as payment of your insurance deductible). Avoid contractors who cannot provide specific cost and schedule details in writing. Note that while indoor air or surface testing can be helpful in some circumstances, no laboratory test can determine definitively that a property is 'safe' — all results must be interpreted in context with environmental conditions.

question_text: What can I do to make the air inside my home safer with all the smoke and ash outside?
official_question: What can I do to make the air inside my home safer with all the smoke and ash outside?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose home was not destroyed wants to know practical steps to improve the air quality inside their home during and after the wildfire event.

source_answer.official_answer: Keep doors and windows closed on windy days, when air quality is poor or unhealthy, and during debris removal activities in your area. Use HEPA air purifiers in frequently used rooms to reduce smoke particles indoors. Upgrade your HVAC system filters to a MERV 13 or higher rating — this significantly improves capture of fine particles — and run the system on recirculate mode rather than drawing in outside air. Avoid activities that generate indoor smoke or fine particles, such as burning candles, using fireplaces, vaping, or frying food at high heat. Monitor air quality using publicly available apps or websites that report the Air Quality Index (AQI) for your area. When air quality improves and outdoor conditions are good, you can open windows briefly to ventilate, but close them again if conditions worsen. Consider cleaning or replacing ductwork if significant ash or soot entered the HVAC system during the event.
required_answer_elements: Advise keeping windows and doors closed during poor air quality and debris removal activity.

Advise avoiding indoor combustion sources (candles, fireplaces, high-heat frying) that worsen indoor air.

Promising any combination of measures eliminates all wildfire-related indoor air risk.

question_text: I've been cleaning up and now I have a cough and my eyes burn. What should I do?
official_question: I've been cleaning up and now I have a cough and my eyes burn. What should I do?
normalized_resident_need: A resident who has been cleaning ash or debris develops symptoms such as coughing, eye irritation, or headaches and wants to know what steps to take.

source_answer.official_answer: Common symptoms of smoke and ash exposure include coughing, wheezing, eye irritation, headaches, and difficulty breathing. If you notice these symptoms during or after cleanup: stop what you are doing and move to an area with cleaner air immediately. If indoors, move to a room with HEPA air filtration. Wash exposed skin and change your clothes to remove any contaminants on your body. For mild symptoms that resolve quickly in clean air, rest and continue to monitor. For symptoms that persist, worsen, or are severe — particularly for individuals with preexisting conditions such as asthma, heart disease, or chronic lung conditions — consult a healthcare provider. Children, elderly individuals, pregnant persons, and those with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions should take extra precautions and speak with their healthcare provider before resuming cleanup activities. If you experience difficulty breathing, chest pain, or other emergency symptoms, call 911.

source_answer.official_answer: Mold can begin growing within 24–48 hours in damp environments, making prompt drying of water-damaged areas essential. Remove standing water as quickly as possible using pumps, wet-dry vacuums, or towels. Use dehumidifiers and fans to remove residual moisture from walls, floors, and furnishings. Clean hard surfaces — such as non-porous walls, floors, and countertops — with a solution of 1 cup of household bleach to 1 gallon of water, allowing it to dry completely. Remove and replace water-damaged porous materials that cannot be adequately dried: this includes drywall, insulation, and carpeting. Do not paint or caulk over mold — it must be removed first. If you discover significant mold growth (typically more than 10 square feet), or if individuals in the household have respiratory conditions or mold sensitivity, consult a professional remediation contractor rather than attempting DIY cleanup. Wear protective gear (N95 mask, gloves, goggles) when cleaning mold or water-damaged areas.

question_text: There's stagnant water pooling on my property after the fire. Should I be worried about mosquitoes?
official_question: There's stagnant water pooling on my property after the fire. Should I be worried about mosquitoes?
normalized_resident_need: A resident has stagnant water accumulating on their fire-damaged property and wants to know whether mosquitoes are a health risk and how to address it.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes. Stagnant water in pools, fountains, overturned containers, clogged gutters, or other areas left by firefighting or rainfall can attract mosquitoes and create breeding habitat for species that may spread diseases including West Nile Virus. Remove or drain standing water wherever possible. For water that cannot be drained — such as ornamental ponds, water features, or damaged pools — use mosquito dunks (tablets containing the biological larvicide Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis, or Bti) to kill mosquito larvae without harming people, pets, or wildlife. Mosquito fish (Gambusia affinis) can also be introduced to larger water bodies to control larvae. Keep gutters clear so water does not pool. Contact the Los Angeles County West Vector and Vector-Borne Disease Control District at westnile.lacounty.gov or by calling 562-944-9888 for assistance with mosquito control on your property.

Recommend draining all standing water where possible.
Mention mosquito dunks (Bti) as a safe treatment option for water that cannot be drained.

question_text: My TV, laptop, and appliances got covered in smoke and soot. How do I clean them?
official_question: My TV, laptop, and appliances got covered in smoke and soot. How do I clean them?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose electronics and appliances were exposed to wildfire smoke and soot wants to know how to safely clean them and when professional help is needed.

source_answer.official_answer: For electronics and appliances exposed to smoke or soot: first, turn off and unplug all devices immediately. Use a soft dry cloth or soft brush to gently remove loose soot and ash from exterior surfaces. Do not use liquid cleaners or spray directly on electronics, as moisture can cause further damage. For small kitchen appliances such as toasters, blenders, or coffee makers, dampen a cloth lightly with water and a small amount of dish soap to wipe exterior surfaces only, avoiding getting any moisture inside the appliance. If in doubt, consider replacing the appliance. If a device was exposed to water (from firefighting efforts) or has significant soot contamination internally, do not attempt to power it on — have it professionally inspected before use. Fire heat can cause internal damage that is not visible externally. Smoke and soot can also cause corrosion inside electronics over time; devices that initially appear functional may develop problems later. For valuable or complex electronics, professional inspection and cleaning is strongly recommended before reuse.
required_answer_elements: Advise turning off and unplugging all devices immediately.
Recommend using a soft dry cloth or brush for exterior cleaning only.
Warn against powering on any device exposed to water or with significant internal soot contamination without professional inspection first.
Note that internal damage from heat may not be visible and professional inspection is recommended for valuable devices.
forbidden_claims: Recommending specific electronic cleaning products by brand.
Promising that exterior cleaning restores device safety.
Telling the user a device that powers on is definitely safe to continue using after smoke exposure.
Recommending the use of compressed air to blow out internal soot (can drive particles deeper into components).

question_text: I found some family photos and heirlooms in the debris. How do I clean and save them?
official_question: I found some family photos and heirlooms in the debris. How do I clean and save them?
normalized_resident_need: A resident has recovered family photos or sentimental items from fire debris and wants to know how to clean and preserve them without causing further damage.

source_answer.official_answer: For photos and keepsakes recovered from fire debris or smoke-exposed areas: if items have only light soot, carefully wipe away loose particles with a soft, dry brush — do not use wet methods on photographic prints until you know whether they are stable, as water can cause ink to run or emulsions to deteriorate. If items are wet or have heavy smoke odor, place them in a clean plastic bag and freeze them to halt further deterioration until you can arrange proper cleaning or restoration — freezing can stabilize wet photos for weeks without causing additional damage. Do not stack wet or sooty photos together, as they can fuse. Allow items to air dry in a clean, well-ventilated area only if they are not currently at risk of fusing. For valuable or irreplaceable items, consult a professional photo restoration service or conservator. Items such as documents, film negatives, and artwork may require specialized handling beyond the scope of home cleaning. Wear gloves and an N95 mask when handling items recovered from fire debris, even keepsakes.

Recommend professional photo restoration services for valuable or irreplaceable items.
Remind the user to wear gloves and N95 when handling items from fire debris.

question_text: FEMA didn't approve me or gave me less than I expected. How do I actually file an appeal?
official_question: FEMA didn't approve me or gave me less than I expected. How do I actually file an appeal?
normalized_resident_need: A FEMA applicant has received a determination letter they want to challenge and needs to know the specific steps to file a written appeal within the 60-day window.

source_answer.official_answer: You have 60 days from the date on your FEMA determination letter to file a written appeal. To appeal: write a signed letter explaining why you believe FEMA's decision is incorrect and what assistance you believe you need. Include your full name, current address, damaged property address, FEMA registration number, and the last four digits of your Social Security number. Attach supporting documentation — this may include contractor repair estimates, receipts, insurance denial or settlement letters, medical records (if claiming medical needs), or other evidence supporting your case. You can submit your appeal by mail to: FEMA National Processing Service Center, P.O. Box 10055, Hyattsville, MD 20782-8055; by fax to 1-800-827-8112; or by uploading documents online at DisasterAssistance.gov or through the FEMA mobile app. If you have insurance, FEMA generally cannot provide assistance for costs your insurance covers — but if your insurance settlement is delayed or insufficient, include documentation of that in your appeal. You can also get free help preparing your appeal at a Disaster Recovery Center.

question_text: I've never used food stamps before, but I lost my job in the fire. Can I apply for CalFresh now?
official_question: I've never used food stamps before, but I lost my job in the fire. Can I apply for CalFresh now?
normalized_resident_need: A resident who has not previously used food assistance programs has experienced income loss due to the Eaton Fire and wants to know whether they now qualify for CalFresh and how to apply.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes. CalFresh (California's Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, SNAP) provides monthly food benefits to low-income households and may now be available to you if your income has been reduced or eliminated due to the Eaton Fire disaster. Apply online at benefitscal.com, in person at your local LA County Department of Public Social Services (DPSS) office, or by calling the CalFresh hotline at 1-877-847-3663. The application asks about your household size, income, expenses, and housing costs. If approved, benefits are loaded onto an EBT card that can be used at grocery stores and some farmers markets. For the fastest possible determination, online applications at benefitscal.com are generally processed quickly. If your income has dropped to zero due to fire-related job loss, note that Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) — see packet DUA_001 — can provide income replacement while CalFresh provides food support; the two programs can be used together.

question_text: I need cash now for food and rent. Are there any emergency cash assistance programs I can get quickly?
official_question: I need cash now for food and rent. Are there any emergency cash assistance programs I can get quickly?
normalized_resident_need: A resident affected by the Eaton Fire needs immediate cash assistance for basic needs such as food, rent, or transportation and wants to know what programs are available.

source_answer.official_answer: Several programs may provide immediate cash or financial assistance to residents affected by the Eaton Fire. General Relief (GR) is an LA County cash assistance program for adults who are ineligible for federal programs and have little or no income — apply at your local DPSS office or at dpss.lacounty.gov. Disaster-affected residents should also apply for FEMA Individual Assistance (DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362), which can provide grants for housing and other needs; FEMA's Serious Needs Assistance program may offer a one-time $770 payment for emergency supplies (see packet FEMA_SNA_001). If your income loss stems from a job affected by the fire, apply for Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) through myEDD at myedd.edd.ca.gov. Community organizations and nonprofit disaster relief funds — including the American Red Cross and United Way of Greater Los Angeles — may also provide immediate emergency financial assistance without the eligibility requirements of government programs. Dial 2-1-1 or visit 211la.org to connect with local emergency financial resources in your area.

question_text: What should I photograph and document before cleaning up, so my insurance claim goes smoothly?
official_question: What should I photograph and document before cleaning up, so my insurance claim goes smoothly?
normalized_resident_need: A resident affected by the Eaton Fire wants to know what to document before cleaning up in order to support a homeowners or renters insurance claim.

source_answer.official_answer: Document all damage thoroughly before undertaking any cleanup or remediation — insurers generally cannot reimburse damage they cannot verify. Take clear photographs and video of all damaged areas and belongings, including structures, contents, outdoor areas, fencing, and landscaping. question_text: My fence burned and my trees are dead. Does my homeowners insurance cover that?
official_question: My fence burned and my trees are dead. Does my homeowners insurance cover that?
normalized_resident_need: A homeowner whose fence, trees, or detached structures were damaged or destroyed by the Eaton Fire wants to know whether their homeowners insurance policy covers these losses.

source_answer.official_answer: Coverage for damage to fencing, landscaping, and detached structures (such as garages, sheds, and guest houses) depends on the specific terms of your homeowners insurance policy. Many standard homeowners policies do include coverage for: detached structures (typically called 'other structures coverage,' often up to 10% of the dwelling coverage limit); fencing; and in some cases landscaping and trees, though tree and shrub coverage often has sub-limits and may only cover trees damaged by specific named perils. To understand what your policy covers, review your declarations page and policy documents, or contact your insurer directly. Keep all receipts and document all damage before cleanup or removal. question_text: My mortgage isn't FHA or VA — it's a regular bank loan. Can I still get help with my payments?
official_question: My mortgage isn't FHA or VA — it's a regular bank loan. Can I still get help with my payments?
normalized_resident_need: A homeowner with a conventional (private, non-government-backed) mortgage is struggling to make payments due to fire damage and wants to know what options are available when the automatic federal forbearance protections do not apply.

source_answer.official_answer: Homeowners with conventional (non-government-backed) mortgages do not have automatic disaster forbearance protections the way FHA, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac borrowers do. However, many private mortgage servicers are voluntarily offering forbearance and other relief to disaster-affected borrowers. The most important step is to contact your mortgage servicer — the company listed on your mortgage statement — as soon as possible and explain that your property was affected by the Eaton Fire disaster. Ask specifically about: forbearance (temporary pause or reduction of payments), loan modification options, and any disaster-specific relief your servicer is offering. California law requires mortgage servicers to respond to borrower hardship requests. HUD-approved housing counselors can help you navigate this conversation at no cost: find one at hud.gov/findacounselor or by calling 1-800-569-4287. As with all loans, do not simply stop making payments without first arranging forbearance with your servicer, as missed payments can result in late fees, credit damage, or foreclosure proceedings.

question_text: Can I park an RV on my lot and live in it while my house is being rebuilt?
official_question: Can I park an RV on my lot and live in it while my house is being rebuilt?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner whose home was destroyed wants to know whether they can legally place and live in an RV or mobile home on their lot while awaiting rebuilding.

source_answer.official_answer: A process for approval of temporary housing — such as RVs or mobile homes — for property owners to stay on or near their property within the fire perimeter area is being developed by LA County. Typically, the approval process requires: ensuring proper wastewater disposal (by utilizing an existing septic system or contracting with a licensed sewage pumping service); submitting the necessary applications and inspection reports to the LA County Land Use Program; ensuring potable water is available; and adhering to zoning or planning requirements for temporary structures. Contact LA County Regional Planning at planning.lacounty.gov or the Altadena Disaster Recovery Center for the most current process and application requirements, as procedures may evolve during the recovery period. Temporary housing placements are generally subject to time limits and cannot proceed until the debris removal process allows safe access to the property.

question_text: What can I do to make my rebuilt home more resistant to future wildfires?
official_question: What can I do to make my rebuilt home more resistant to future wildfires?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner rebuilding after the Eaton Fire wants to know what construction choices will make their new home more resistant to future wildfires.

source_answer.official_answer: Rebuilding after the Eaton Fire offers an opportunity to make your home significantly more fire-resistant. Key measures include: roofing — use Class A fire-rated roofing materials; vents — install ember-resistant vents (such as those meeting California Building Code requirements for the Wildland-Urban Interface), as embers entering through vents are a leading cause of home ignition; siding and exterior walls — use non-combustible or ignition-resistant materials such as stucco, fiber cement, or brick; decks and eaves — enclosed eaves and non-combustible deck materials reduce ember accumulation; windows — dual-pane or tempered glass is more resistant to radiant heat than single-pane; and defensible space — create and maintain at least 30 feet of clear, fuel-reduced zone around the home, with Zone 1 (0–30 ft) being lean, clean, and green, and Zone 2 (30–100 ft) having reduced fuel loads. Like-for-like rebuilds in the Eaton Fire area are subject to current Building Code and Fire Code even while receiving Zoning Code exemptions (see REBUILD_LIKEFORLIKE_001). Consult with LA County Regional Planning and the LA County Fire Department for project-specific fire hardening requirements.

Note that like-for-like rebuilds must still comply with current Building and Fire Codes.

question_text: My yard is bare and scorched. How do I prevent erosion and restore my landscaping?
official_question: My yard is bare and scorched. How do I prevent erosion and restore my landscaping?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner in the Eaton Fire burn area has bare, scorched ground and wants to know how to stabilize soil, prevent erosion, and begin restoring their landscaping.

source_answer.official_answer: Wildfire removes the vegetation that holds soil in place, making burned hillsides and yards vulnerable to erosion, mudslides, and debris flows — especially during rain events. To stabilize soil and reduce erosion: apply organic mulch (wood chips or straw) over bare soil to slow runoff and hold moisture; add compost or organic matter to rebuild soil structure and nutrients; plant fire-resistant, native vegetation that will establish quickly and hold soil; cover bare areas with erosion control blankets or jute netting on slopes if re-planting is not immediately possible; and avoid using ash as a soil amendment, as it may contain harmful contaminants including heavy metals. Consult your local UC Cooperative Extension office for plant recommendations suited to your area and for guidance on erosion control measures appropriate to your slope and soil type. In Eaton Fire areas, contact LA County Public Works for guidance on large-scale erosion control on significantly burned hillside properties. Be aware that rain events following wildfires can cause rapid debris flows in burn scars — monitor weather and heed any debris flow or flood watches issued for your area.

question_text: My well or water tank was damaged in the fire. Is my water safe to use?
official_question: My well or water tank was damaged in the fire. Is my water safe to use?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner whose private well or water storage tank was damaged or potentially contaminated during the Eaton Fire wants to know whether their water is safe and what steps to take.

source_answer.official_answer: Do not use water from a well or water storage tank that was damaged, exposed to fire, or located on a property that has not yet completed debris removal, until the water has been tested and confirmed safe. Wildfires can introduce harmful bacteria, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and other chemicals into groundwater and storage tanks through damaged casings, melted components, or firefighting chemical runoff. Inspect the well or tank visually for obvious damage such as cracks, burned or melted components, and document with photographs. Do not attempt repairs until Phase 2 debris removal is complete and your property has been cleared for rebuilding. Once cleared, hire a licensed contractor for repairs and inspection. Have the water tested for contaminants by a certified lab before use — ask specifically for testing for bacteria (total coliform and E. coli), VOCs, and heavy metals. To obtain a Water Availability Letter for rebuilding purposes, submit proof of your water source (utility bill, well report, or letter from a potable water hauler) to the LA County Drinking Water Program; additional testing or inspections may be required. Contact the LA County Department of Public Health at (626) 430-5380 for guidance.

question_text: My house is still standing but it was in the fire zone. How do I know if it's structurally safe?
official_question: My house is still standing but it was in the fire zone. How do I know if it's structurally safe?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner whose home was within the fire zone but appears intact wants to know how to determine whether it is structurally safe before entering or reoccupying it.

source_answer.official_answer: Structural integrity after wildfire exposure must be assessed by a licensed structural engineer or a qualified contractor, not by visual inspection alone. Fire can weaken structural elements — including foundations, load-bearing walls, beams, and fasteners — without leaving obvious visible signs. Do not enter or reoccupy a building that has been red-tagged by LA County building inspectors (a red placard means the structure is unsafe and entry is prohibited). Yellow-tagged buildings may allow limited entry for specific purposes; consult the tag for conditions. For buildings that appear undamaged but were within the fire perimeter, a licensed professional can evaluate foundations for cracking or heat damage, walls and framing for warping or charring, and critical structural connections for heat-induced weakening. Obtain a detailed written inspection report before making decisions about repair, rebuilding, or reoccupancy. Structural inspections may also be required before building permits are issued. Some insurance policies cover the cost of a structural assessment — check with your insurer.

Recommend obtaining a written inspection report before reoccupying or making repair decisions.
Note that structural inspections may be required before permits are issued.

Recommending entry into a red-tagged building for any reason.

question_text: We lost power for several days from the Eaton fire. Which food in my fridge and freezer is still safe to eat?
official_question: We lost power for several days from the Eaton fire. Which food in my fridge and freezer is still safe to eat?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose home lost power during or after the Eaton Fire wants to know which refrigerated and frozen foods are safe to eat and which should be discarded.

source_answer.official_answer: The general food safety rule for power outages is: discard any perishable items in the refrigerator that were without power for more than 4 hours. Refrigerators keep food safe for about 4 hours if kept closed; a full freezer maintains safe temperature for about 48 hours (24 hours if half full) if kept closed. When in doubt, throw it out — do not taste food to determine whether it is safe, as foodborne pathogens do not always change the smell, appearance, or taste of food. Items that are typically safe include: hard cheeses (not soft), fruit juices, opened fruit and vegetable juices (if refrigerated), bread, rolls, cakes, muffins, fresh whole fruits and vegetables, and foods that do not require refrigeration. Items that should be discarded after more than 4 hours without refrigeration include: meat, poultry, seafood, milk, soft cheeses, cooked leftovers, eggs, mayonnaise, and creamy sauces. Sealed, commercially canned goods and shelf-stable packaged foods that were not exposed to smoke or ash can generally be kept; rinse cans before opening. If food was exposed to wildfire smoke or ash, or to floodwater, discard it regardless of power status.

Note that food exposed to smoke, ash, or floodwater should be discarded regardless of power status.

question_text: I own a restaurant or food business that was affected by the Eaton fire. What do I need to do before I can reopen?
official_question: I own a restaurant or food business that was affected by the Eaton fire. What do I need to do before I can reopen?
normalized_resident_need: A food service business owner whose establishment was disrupted or damaged by the Eaton Fire wants to know what steps are required before they can legally reopen.

source_answer.official_answer: Before reopening a food service business after wildfire disruption, take the following steps. First, inspect all food storage and preparation areas for signs of smoke, ash, soot, or water damage; replace all contaminated or compromised food and beverages. Sanitize all food-contact equipment and surfaces thoroughly using approved sanitizing solutions. Inspect and test all equipment for proper function, including refrigeration and cooking equipment; do not use equipment that may have been heat-damaged without professional inspection. Verify that utilities — water, gas, and electricity — are fully restored and safe. Contact the LA County Department of Public Health Environmental Health Division to request a pre-reopening inspection: a health inspector must clear your establishment before you resume food service operations. Obtain any required permits or clearances from other agencies (building, fire). Consult the LA County Environmental Health Division at ehservices.lacounty.gov or call (888) 700-9995 for current guidance.

question_text: What is a Disaster Recovery Center? Where are they, and what can they help me with?
official_question: What is a Disaster Recovery Center? Where are they, and what can they help me with?
normalized_resident_need: A resident affected by the Eaton Fire wants to know what a Disaster Recovery Center is, where the nearest one is, what agencies are present, and what help they can get there.

source_answer.official_answer: Disaster Recovery Centers (DRCs) are walk-in locations where residents affected by the Eaton Fire can get in-person help from federal, state, and county agencies. You do not need an appointment. Local Assistance Centers and Disaster Recovery Centers are generally open Monday through Saturday, 9:00 AM to 7:00 PM. Key DRC locations include: Altadena Disaster Recovery Center, 540 West Woodbury Road, Altadena, CA 91001; and Westside Disaster Recovery Center at UCLA Research Park West, 10850 West Pico Blvd., Los Angeles, CA 90064. Federal agencies typically represented on-site include FEMA, the Small Business Administration (SBA), and the IRS. LA County departments on-site may include the Assessor's Office, Department of Consumer and Business Affairs, Department of Mental Health, DPSS (CalFresh, CalWORKs, General Relief, Medi-Cal), Department of Public Health, and others. At a DRC you can: get help applying for FEMA assistance, check your application status, file a FEMA appeal, speak with SBA about disaster loans, receive DMV and vital records assistance, connect with mental health services, and get information on other county and state programs. Bring your government-issued ID and any relevant documentation. There is no charge for DRC services.

official_question: What is a Disaster Recovery Center? Where are they, and what can they help me with?
normalized_resident_need: A resident affected by the Eaton Fire wants to know what a Disaster Recovery Center is, where the nearest one is, what agencies are present, and what help they can get there.

source_answer.official_answer: Disaster Recovery Centers (DRCs) are walk-in locations where residents affected by the Eaton Fire can get in-person help from federal, state, and county agencies. You do not need an appointment. Local Assistance Centers and Disaster Recovery Centers are generally open Monday through Saturday, 9:00 AM to 7:00 PM. Key DRC locations include: Altadena Disaster Recovery Center, 540 West Woodbury Road, Altadena, CA 91001; and Westside Disaster Recovery Center at UCLA Research Park West, 10850 West Pico Blvd., Los Angeles, CA 90064. Federal agencies typically represented on-site include FEMA, the Small Business Administration (SBA), and the IRS. LA County departments on-site may include the Assessor's Office, Department of Consumer and Business Affairs, Department of Mental Health, DPSS (CalFresh, CalWORKs, General Relief, Medi-Cal), Department of Public Health, and others. At a DRC you can: get help applying for FEMA assistance, check your application status, file a FEMA appeal, speak with SBA about disaster loans, receive DMV and vital records assistance, connect with mental health services, and get information on other county and state programs. Bring your government-issued ID and any relevant documentation. There is no charge for DRC services.

question_text: Contractors keep showing up at my house offering to help after the fire. How do I know if they're legitimate?
official_question: Contractors keep showing up at my house offering to help after the fire. How do I know if they're legitimate?
normalized_resident_need: A disaster-affected homeowner is being approached by contractors offering cleanup and repair services and wants to know how to identify legitimate contractors and avoid scams.

source_answer.official_answer: Contractor scams surge after disasters, targeting residents who are desperate to repair or rebuild. Protect yourself with these steps. Verify licensing: all California contractors who perform work worth $500 or more in labor and materials must be licensed by the Contractors State License Board (CSLB). Verify any contractor's license at cslb.ca.gov or call 1-800-321-2752 before signing anything. Require a written contract: never pay for or authorize work without a written contract that specifies the scope of work, materials, timeline, and total cost. Never pay the full amount upfront — standard practice in California is a down payment of no more than 10% of the contract price, or $1,000, whichever is less. Be wary of: door-to-door solicitations; demands for full cash payment upfront; contractors who say they have materials left over from a nearby job; pressure to sign immediately; and contractors who are not local or cannot provide local references. Report suspected unlicensed contractor activity to the CSLB at cslb.ca.gov or 1-800-321-2752. Also report to the California Attorney General at oag.ca.gov or the LA County Department of Consumer and Business Affairs at (800) 593-8222. Predatory investors are also prohibited from making unsolicited undervalue offers to fire-affected property owners; report such offers to the California Department of Real Estate at LAFires@DRE.CA.GOV.

Provide the CSLB license verification method: cslb.ca.gov or 1-800-321-2752.

question_text: My trees are dead or badly burned. Do I need a permit to remove them, and who pays for it?
official_question: My trees are dead or badly burned. Do I need a permit to remove them, and who pays for it?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner has fire-damaged or dead trees on their lot and wants to know whether permits are required, who is responsible, and whether the cost is covered by the debris removal program or insurance.

source_answer.official_answer: Fire-damaged trees that pose an imminent hazard to structures, utilities, or people may be addressed as part of the government debris removal process. Trees within the scope of Phase 2 debris removal — including hazardous trees designated by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers or the opt-out debris removal contractor — may be removed as part of that process. For trees that were not included in the debris removal program or that are on properties that opted out, removal may require permits depending on local ordinances, the size of the tree, and whether it is a protected species. Contact LA County Regional Planning at planning.lacounty.gov or your local jurisdiction for permit requirements before removing large or protected trees. Property owners are generally responsible for costs of tree removal not covered by the government debris removal program; homeowners insurance may cover tree removal if the tree has damaged a structure — check your policy. If a damaged tree is threatening a neighboring property, contact your insurer and consult LA County's Department of Consumer and Business Affairs for guidance on liability.

State that tree removal outside the debris removal program may require permits depending on local ordinances and tree species.
Direct the user to LA County Regional Planning for permit requirements.
Note that homeowners insurance may cover removal of trees that damaged structures.
forbidden_claims: Telling the user all fire-damaged trees will be removed by the government at no cost.
Telling the user no permits are required for removing dead trees.
Inventing specific permit fees.
Guaranteeing insurance will cover tree removal costs.

question_text: I have Medi-Cal but I lost my card and all my documents in the fire. Can I still see a doctor?
official_question: I have Medi-Cal but I lost my card and all my documents in the fire. Can I still see a doctor?
normalized_resident_need: A Medi-Cal recipient who lost their card and identification in the Eaton Fire wants to know how to continue accessing healthcare and how to replace their coverage documents.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes. If you have Medi-Cal coverage, you can continue to access healthcare services even if you lost your Medi-Cal card, ID, or documents in the fire. Providers can verify your coverage using your name and date of birth or Social Security number. To get a replacement Medi-Cal Benefits Identification Card (BIC), contact your county DPSS office or call the Medi-Cal Member Help Line at 1-800-541-5555. LA County DPSS offices and Disaster Recovery Centers have representatives on-site who can assist with Medi-Cal continuity and replacement cards. If your income or household circumstances have changed due to the fire — for example, if you lost your job — you may also be newly eligible for Medi-Cal; apply through Covered California at coveredca.com or at benefitscal.com. If you need prescription medications and cannot access your pharmacy or prescriptions, the Emergency Prescription Assistance Program (EPAP) may be able to help uninsured or underinsured individuals — ask at a Disaster Recovery Center.

official_question: I don't have a car and I need to get to a Disaster Recovery Center or doctor after Eaton fire in LA. How can I get transportation help?
normalized_resident_need: A disaster survivor without a vehicle or with mobility limitations needs transportation to reach a Disaster Recovery Center, shelter, medical appointment, or other disaster-related resource.

source_answer.official_answer: Several transportation options are available for Eaton Fire survivors without access to a vehicle. Call 211 (2-1-1 by phone or 211la.org) — LA's social services referral line — to ask about transportation assistance programs available in your area, including rides to Disaster Recovery Centers, medical appointments, and shelters. Many nonprofit organizations activated in disaster responses also offer ride assistance; 211 can connect you with current programs. LA Metro continues to operate bus and rail service throughout the region; LA Metro also has a reduced-fare program for qualifying low-income riders and seniors. People with disabilities or qualifying medical conditions may be eligible for Access Services paratransit — contact Access Services at 1-800-827-0829. FEMA Individual Assistance grants may include transportation costs as a component of disaster-related needs; document your transportation expenses and include them in your FEMA application. The LA County Department of Aging and Disabilities may also provide transportation support for older adults and people with disabilities; contact them through the DRC or at aging.lacounty.gov.

question_text: After going through this Eaton fire, how do I better prepare my family for a future evacuation?
official_question: After going through this Eaton fire, how do I better prepare my family for a future evacuation?
normalized_resident_need: A resident who experienced the Eaton Fire evacuation wants to be better prepared for future wildfire events and wants concrete, actionable steps to take before the next emergency.

source_answer.official_answer: Preparedness steps that will make future evacuations faster and safer include: Emergency kit: assemble a 'go-bag' with at least 72 hours of supplies per person, including water (one gallon per person per day), non-perishable food, prescription medications, copies of important documents (ID, insurance policies, FEMA registration number), phone charger and backup battery, N95 masks, and sturdy shoes. Important documents: store copies of vital records — ID, insurance cards, Social Security cards, medical records, financial account information — in a fireproof safe and back up digital copies to cloud storage. Family plan: establish a meeting point outside your neighborhood, a designated out-of-area contact, and a plan for pets and any family members with mobility limitations. Sign up for alerts: register for LA County's emergency alert system at alert.lacounty.gov; this provides mandatory evacuation orders and warnings to your phone and email. Know your evacuation zone: look up your property's evacuation zone at lavote.gov or lacounty.gov so you know when an order applies to you. Defensible space: maintain at least 30 feet of cleared, fire-resistant vegetation around your home year-round. Financial preparedness: photograph or video your home's contents annually for insurance documentation purposes.

question_text: Do I have to pay permit fees to rebuild after the Eaton Fire? I heard they were waived.
official_question: Do I have to pay permit fees to rebuild after the Eaton Fire? I heard they were waived.
normalized_resident_need: A property owner planning to rebuild after the Eaton Fire wants to know whether permit fees are waived, who qualifies, and what fees to expect if they do not qualify.

source_answer.official_answer: On June 17, 2025, the LA County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a motion to waive and refund permit fees for qualifying property owners rebuilding single-family homes in unincorporated Los Angeles County following the Eaton and Palisades wildfires. To qualify for the fee waiver and refund, the property owner must have both owned and lived in the property being rebuilt prior to January 7, 2025. Waived fees include: Zoning Review Fees, Building Plan Review Fees, Soils/Geological Review Fees (if applicable), Building Permit and Inspection Fees, and Fire Department Plan Review Fees. For property owners who do not qualify for the waiver, estimated fee costs include: Regional Planning fees of $1,429 for like-for-like rebuild projects and $1,623 for non-like-for-like projects not requiring a public hearing; Building and Safety plan check and permit fees that vary by project size (approximately $22,000 for a 3,000 sq ft home; approximately $12,000 for a 1,500 sq ft home); Fire Department fees including a $565 building plan review fee, a $565 fire sprinkler plan review fee, and a fuel modification plan review fee of $735 (homes under 2,500 sq ft) or $845 (homes over 2,500 sq ft). Standing homes that were damaged but not destroyed may qualify for a fee deferral on a case-by-case basis — contact a One-Stop Permit Center at recovery.lacounty.gov/rebuilding/one-stop-permit-centers or email recovery@planning.lacounty.gov.

question_text: Can I build a small unit — an ADU — on my lot and live in it while I wait for my house to be rebuilt after the Eaton Fire?
official_question: Can I build a small unit — an ADU — on my lot and live in it while I wait for my house to be rebuilt after the Eaton Fire?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner whose home was destroyed wants to build an ADU on their lot as a place to live during the rebuild process and wants to know if this is allowed and what the rules are.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes. LA County allows a new, standalone Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) to be built on a fire-affected property and occupied by the household while the primary dwelling unit is being rebuilt on the same property. The household may temporarily occupy the standalone ADU until January 7, 2030. The ADU will not be considered a temporary structure and will not need to be removed from the property at a future date — it can remain as a permanent accessory unit. LA County staff will require an application and permits for the new ADU, and these will be expedited through the recovery permitting process. The new ADU must comply with current Zoning Code and State law requirements, as well as current Building Code, Fire Code, and Health and Safety Code requirements. ADUs are subject to permit fees (or the fee waiver if the property owner qualifies — see PERMIT_FEES_001).

question_text: My foundation looks intact. Do I have to tear it out, or can I build on top of it?
official_question: My foundation looks intact. Do I have to tear it out, or can I build on top of it?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner believes their foundation survived the fire and wants to know whether they can reuse it for the rebuild rather than requiring full demolition and replacement.

source_answer.official_answer: You may be able to reuse your existing foundation if it is found to be suitable, but this must be determined by a licensed engineering professional — not by visual inspection alone. To pursue foundation reuse: retain a licensed civil engineer, structural engineer, or architect to evaluate the foundation and determine whether it can be reused. If the design professional determines the foundation suffered minimal fire damage, it may be used in new construction provided it meets current building code requirements. The determination must be based on thorough testing and forensic analysis. The engineer must complete the LA County form 'Reuse of Existing Foundation Systems in a Fire Damaged Structure (Rev 02-2025),' available from LA County Public Works. The design professional must also verify that all under-slab utility systems — drainage, waste, vent, water, mechanical, and electrical — are suitable for continued use. If the foundation is not removed during debris removal but is later found to be unsuitable, a separate demolition permit will be required to remove it. Contact LA County Building and Safety or your One-Stop Permit Center for more information.

question_text: I have oak trees on my property that were damaged by the fire. Can I remove them to rebuild?
official_question: I have oak trees on my property that were damaged by the fire. Can I remove them to rebuild?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner with oak trees on their fire-affected lot wants to know whether they can remove damaged or dead-looking oak trees during the rebuild process.

source_answer.official_answer: Damaged oak trees generally cannot be removed, even after the fire, because fire-damaged oak trees may resprout within a two-year monitoring period and should be given time to recover. However, if an oak tree is deemed a hazard by the LA County Forester, it may be removed with a valid Oak Tree Permit Exemption. For like-for-like rebuild projects: these do not need to comply with current Zoning Code requirements, including the Oak Tree Ordinance. However, no oak trees can be removed. If the original structure encroached into the protected zone of an oak tree, the like-for-like replacement structure cannot encroach further into the protected zone. For non-like-for-like rebuild projects: the project must comply with current Zoning Code requirements, including the Oak Tree Ordinance. Contact LA County Regional Planning for guidance on the Oak Tree Ordinance and Oak Tree Permit requirements specific to your property before making any decisions about oak trees.

question_text: Do I have to use electric appliances when I rebuild? Can I keep my gas stove and fireplace?
official_question: Do I have to use electric appliances when I rebuild? Can I keep my gas stove and fireplace?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner rebuilding after the Eaton Fire wants to know whether they are required to install electric-only appliances and whether they can have a wood-burning fireplace.

source_answer.official_answer: For Eaton Fire rebuilds: current code requires a new building to be 'electric ready,' meaning it must have the electrical infrastructure to accommodate electric appliances, but you are still allowed to install gas appliances. You are not required to switch from gas to all-electric. Regarding chimneys and fireplaces: the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD) has waived the previous requirement that chimneys in new construction be gas-burning only. As a result, wood-burning chimneys are now allowed for all Eaton Fire rebuild projects. Check with your assigned land use planner or LA County Regional Planning at planning.lacounty.gov for current requirements on your specific project, as conditions may evolve during the recovery period.

question_text: Do I have to connect to the sewer when I rebuild, or can I keep using my septic?
official_question: Do I have to connect to the sewer when I rebuild, or can I keep using my septic?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner on septic wants to know whether they will be required to connect to the county sewer system when they rebuild, and what the rules are for keeping their existing septic.

source_answer.official_answer: Whether you are required to connect to the county sewer depends on your property's location relative to existing sewer infrastructure. If your proposed building is within 200 linear feet of a sewer main without crossing a neighbor's property, the LA County Department of Public Health cannot issue a permit to construct or repair a septic system. However, you may rebuild using your existing septic system if: the system is in good working order, and you are rebuilding with the same number of units and bedrooms for which the septic system was originally approved. If you intend to add a bedroom, pool, Accessory Dwelling Unit, or other change that increases wastewater flow, you will be required to upgrade your septic system to meet current standards. An exemption to the sewer connection requirement may be available from the Department of Public Works if your property cannot practically connect to the sewer — for example, if the sewer line is located on a street above your property. LA County is also analyzing the feasibility of extending sewer service to Altadena neighborhoods that are currently on septic; contact LA County Public Works for current information on your neighborhood. Reconstruction of a single-family residence is not subject to Sanitation District fees if the property was already on sewer.

State that adding bedrooms, ADUs, or other wastewater-increasing changes requires septic system upgrade.

question_text: My original house was right on the property line. Will I have to set back the new one farther?
official_question: My original house was right on the property line. Will I have to set back the new one farther?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner whose original home did not conform to current setback requirements wants to know whether they can rebuild in the same footprint or must comply with current setback rules.

source_answer.official_answer: Like-for-like replacement structures can have the same setbacks as the legally established damaged or destroyed structure and do not need to comply with current setback requirements. This means that if your original home had a setback that does not conform to current zoning standards, a like-for-like rebuild can maintain that same non-conforming setback. If your rebuild project does not meet Regional Planning's like-for-like standards, the new structure will need to comply with current setback requirements. A property owner can request modifications to current setback requirements for non-like-for-like projects, but such requests require a public hearing and approval is not guaranteed. For all rebuild projects in the Eaton Fire area, the minimum required front yard setback is 20 feet; the Altadena Community Standards District front yard setback requirements are suspended for rebuild projects. Contact LA County Regional Planning at planning.lacounty.gov for project-specific guidance.

question_text: I heard there are special fire-resistant building requirements for homes in high-fire-risk areas. Do they apply to my rebuild?
official_question: I heard there are special fire-resistant building requirements for homes in high-fire-risk areas. Do they apply to my rebuild?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner is planning to rebuild and wants to know whether special fire-resistant construction requirements apply to their project given the property's location in or near the Eaton Fire burn area.

source_answer.official_answer: California designates certain geographic areas as Fire Hazard Severity Zones (FHSZs), classified as Very High, High, or Moderate risk. The Eaton Fire area includes properties in Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) Fire Areas and Fire Hazard Severity Zones. Chapter 7A of the California Building Code applies to all new buildings and to additions, alterations, and repairs made to existing buildings within these zones. The purpose of Chapter 7A is to establish minimum standards for building materials and construction methods that increase a structure's ability to resist flame intrusion and burning embers from vegetation fires. Requirements under Chapter 7A include standards for roofing, vents, windows, exterior walls, decks, and other components. If your property is in a Fire Hazard Severity Zone or WUI Fire Area — which is likely for many Eaton Fire rebuild properties — your rebuild must comply with Chapter 7A requirements. Even like-for-like rebuilds must comply with current Building Code and Fire Code, including Chapter 7A. Contact LA County Regional Planning at planning.lacounty.gov or the LA County Fire Department for specific requirements applicable to your property.

State that even like-for-like rebuilds must comply with current Building Code including Chapter 7A.

question_text: My house burned down. Do I still have to pay property taxes on a home that no longer exists?
official_question: My house burned down. Do I still have to pay property taxes on a home that no longer exists?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner whose home was destroyed or significantly damaged by the Eaton Fire wants to know whether they can get their property taxes reduced to reflect the damage.

source_answer.official_answer: No. California law (Revenue and Taxation Code Section 170) provides for property tax reassessment relief for properties damaged or destroyed by a disaster. Property owners whose property was damaged or destroyed in the Eaton Fire may apply to the LA County Assessor for a reduction in assessed value reflecting the damage. If approved, your property taxes will be reduced or prorated to reflect the damaged condition of the property. You must file a claim with the LA County Assessor's Office within 12 months of the date of the damage — do not miss this deadline. Once your property is rebuilt and re-assessed, your taxes will return to a level reflecting the new construction. Additionally, under Proposition 19 (effective February 2021), if you are 55 or older, severely disabled, or a wildfire victim, you may be able to transfer your existing assessed value to a replacement property anywhere in California, potentially keeping your pre-fire tax base. Contact the LA County Assessor at assessor.lacounty.gov or (213) 974-3211 for forms and current guidance.

question_text: I can barely afford my utilities now. Are there programs that can help reduce my electricity and gas bills?
official_question: I can barely afford my utilities now. Are there programs that can help reduce my electricity and gas bills?
normalized_resident_need: A household affected by the Eaton Fire is struggling with utility costs and wants to know about programs that can reduce electricity and gas bills.

source_answer.official_answer: Several programs can help lower-income households reduce utility costs, both before and after a disaster. CARE (California Alternate Rates for Energy) provides a discount of approximately 20–35% on electricity bills and 20% on natural gas bills for qualifying low-income households — apply through your utility provider (SoCalGas for gas, Southern California Edison or LADWP for electricity). FERA (Family Electric Rate Assistance) offers an approximately 18% discount on electricity bills for slightly higher-income households with at least three people — apply through your electricity provider. LIHEAP (Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program) provides one-time financial assistance for utility bills to income-qualifying households and may be especially helpful for households facing a crisis bill — apply through LA County DPSS at dpss.lacounty.gov or call 1-877-847-3663. If your home was destroyed, contact your utility provider directly to pause or cancel service and avoid ongoing charges for a property you are no longer occupying. SoCalGas can be reached at 1-800-427-2200; Southern California Edison at 1-800-655-4555.

normalized_resident_need: A household affected by the Eaton Fire is struggling with utility costs and wants to know about programs that can reduce electricity and gas bills.

source_answer.official_answer: Several programs can help lower-income households reduce utility costs, both before and after a disaster. CARE (California Alternate Rates for Energy) provides a discount of approximately 20–35% on electricity bills and 20% on natural gas bills for qualifying low-income households — apply through your utility provider (SoCalGas for gas, Southern California Edison or LADWP for electricity). FERA (Family Electric Rate Assistance) offers an approximately 18% discount on electricity bills for slightly higher-income households with at least three people — apply through your electricity provider. LIHEAP (Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program) provides one-time financial assistance for utility bills to income-qualifying households and may be especially helpful for households facing a crisis bill — apply through LA County DPSS at dpss.lacounty.gov or call 1-877-847-3663. If your home was destroyed, contact your utility provider directly to pause or cancel service and avoid ongoing charges for a property you are no longer occupying. SoCalGas can be reached at 1-800-427-2200; Southern California Edison at 1-800-655-4555.
required_answer_elements: Describe CARE as a 20–35% electricity discount and 20% gas discount for qualifying low-income households.
Describe FERA as an approximately 18% electricity discount for slightly higher-income households with 3+ people.
Mention LIHEAP as a one-time financial assistance program for utility bills through LA County DPSS.
Advise residents whose homes were destroyed to contact their utility provider to pause or cancel service.
forbidden_claims: Inventing specific income thresholds for CARE or FERA eligibility (these vary and change).
Guaranteeing approval for any program.
Stating that disaster-affected households receive automatic utility discounts without applying.
Inventing specific utility provider discount percentages beyond those in the source.
