question_text: My kids can't go back to their school because we had to move. How do I enroll them somewhere new quickly?
official_question: My kids can't go back to their school because we had to move. How do I enroll them somewhere new quickly?
normalized_resident_need: A parent whose children were displaced from their school by the Eaton Fire wants to know how to enroll their children in a new school quickly, especially without having all required documents.

source_answer.official_answer: Children and youth who are displaced from their homes due to the Eaton Fire have protected enrollment rights under the federal McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act. Under McKinney-Vento, displaced children have the right to: immediate enrollment in a new school without waiting for documents such as immunization records, proof of residency, or school records; the right to remain in their original school with transportation assistance provided if feasible; and access to services without stigma or barriers. Schools must enroll displaced children immediately and sort out documentation later. Contact the school district directly and inform them that your child has been displaced by the Eaton Fire — each school district is required to have a McKinney-Vento Homeless Liaison who can assist with enrollment and services. For LAUSD, contact the Office of Student Integration Services. For other LA County school districts, contact the Los Angeles County Office of Education at (562) 922-6111 or lacoe.edu for referral to the appropriate homeless liaison. Displaced students are also entitled to free meals through the National School Lunch Program if the family's income situation has changed.
required_answer_elements: State that displaced children have immediate enrollment rights under the McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act — schools must enroll without waiting for documents.
State that displaced children may also have the right to remain in their original school with transportation assistance.
Direct the user to the school district's McKinney-Vento Homeless Liaison for assistance.
Provide the LA County Office of Education contact for referrals: (562) 922-6111 or lacoe.edu.
forbidden_claims: Telling the user they must provide immunization records or proof of residency before a child can be enrolled.
Telling the user McKinney-Vento does not apply because the family is staying in a hotel or with relatives (displacement qualifies).
Inventing district-specific enrollment procedures beyond those in the source.
Guaranteeing transportation to the original school will be provided in all cases.

question_text: I'm 72 years old and I can't navigate all of these programs on my own. Is there help specifically for seniors?
official_question: I'm 72 years old and I can't navigate all of these programs on my own. Is there help specifically for seniors?
normalized_resident_need: An older adult affected by the Eaton Fire is overwhelmed by the number of programs and processes and wants to know what senior-specific resources and assistance are available.

source_answer.official_answer: Several resources specifically support older adults affected by the Eaton Fire. LA County Department of Aging and Disabilities has representatives available at Disaster Recovery Centers who can provide case management and connect seniors to programs — visit a DRC at 540 W. Woodbury Rd., Altadena or 10850 W. Pico Blvd., Los Angeles. For services including meal delivery, transportation, and in-home support, call the LA County Senior Information Line at 1-800-510-2020 or dial 211. Seniors who have difficulty navigating applications may also call FEMA's help line at 1-800-621-3362 and ask for additional assistance — FEMA provides accessible formats and in-person help at Disaster Recovery Centers. For transportation to recovery centers, medical appointments, and shelter, Access Services paratransit is available at 1-800-827-0829 for eligible older adults and people with disabilities. CalFresh, General Relief, and Medi-Cal applications can all be completed in person at DPSS offices with help from staff. The Ombudsman Program (1-800-334-9473) can also assist seniors in care facilities who have been affected by the disaster.

question_text: I need legal help — my landlord is trying to kick me out and my insurance denied my claim. Can I get a free lawyer?
official_question: I need legal help — my landlord is trying to kick me out and my insurance denied my claim. Can I get a free lawyer?
normalized_resident_need: A disaster survivor is facing legal problems related to insurance, landlord disputes, FEMA appeals, or contractor issues and wants to know how to access free legal help.

source_answer.official_answer: Free legal assistance is available to Eaton Fire survivors through several programs. FEMA's Disaster Legal Services (DLS) program, operated in partnership with the American Bar Association (ABA) Young Lawyers Division, provides free civil legal help to low-income disaster survivors. To access DLS, call the FEMA helpline at 1-800-621-3362. Common issues DLS can help with include: insurance claims and denials, FEMA appeals, landlord-tenant disputes, replacement of legal documents, and contractor disputes. The LA County Bar Association Lawyer Referral and Information Service also operates a reduced-fee referral program: call (213) 243-1525. The Los Angeles Center for Law and Justice, Neighborhood Legal Services of Los Angeles County, and Bet Tzedek Legal Services also provide free civil legal assistance to low-income residents — contact 211 for referrals to these organizations. For insurance-specific disputes, the California Department of Insurance provides a free mediation program for policyholders: 1-800-927-4357.

question_text: My rental was destroyed by the fire. Am I still on the hook for rent? Can I break the lease?
official_question: My rental was destroyed by the fire. Am I still on the hook for rent? Can I break the lease?
normalized_resident_need: A renter whose unit was destroyed or made uninhabitable by the Eaton Fire wants to know whether they must continue paying rent and whether they can terminate their lease without penalty.

source_answer.official_answer: Under California Civil Code Section 1932, a tenant may terminate a rental agreement if the property becomes substantially uninhabitable due to a disaster or casualty not caused by the tenant. If your rental unit was destroyed or made uninhabitable by the Eaton Fire through no fault of your own, you have the right to vacate and terminate the lease without penalty and without owing further rent after the date you vacated. You do not owe rent for any period during which the unit was uninhabitable. Notify your landlord in writing of your decision to terminate the tenancy and keep a copy. You are entitled to the return of your security deposit, minus any legitimate deductions for damage you caused (not fire damage), within 21 days of vacating. If your unit was only partially affected and you remain in occupancy, you may be entitled to a rent reduction proportional to the loss of use. For help navigating landlord disputes, contact the LA County Department of Consumer and Business Affairs at (800) 593-8222 or dcba.lacounty.gov, or seek free legal assistance through the Disaster Legal Services program (1-800-621-3362).

question_text: My insurance company cancelled my policy before the fire and now I can't get coverage anywhere. What can I do?
official_question: My insurance company cancelled my policy before the fire and now I can't get coverage anywhere. What can I do?
normalized_resident_need: A homeowner in the Eaton Fire area who had their insurance policy cancelled before the fire or cannot obtain coverage wants to know what options exist to get insured.

source_answer.official_answer: The California FAIR Plan Association (FAIR Plan) is the state's insurer of last resort for homeowners who cannot obtain fire insurance through the standard market. If you have been unable to obtain a homeowners insurance policy through private insurers, you have the right to apply for FAIR Plan coverage regardless of your property's fire risk. The FAIR Plan provides basic fire and extended coverage for your dwelling — it does not automatically include all the coverages of a standard homeowners policy, such as liability or personal property protection, but you can purchase companion policies from private insurers to fill those gaps. Apply for FAIR Plan coverage at cfpnet.com or call 1-800-339-4099. Contact the CDI at 1-800-927-4357 for guidance on your specific situation and options.

question_text: My business didn't have any physical damage but I lost a lot of revenue because of the fire and evacuations. Can I get an SBA loan?
official_question: My business didn't have any physical damage but I lost a lot of revenue because of the fire and evacuations. Can I get an SBA loan?
normalized_resident_need: A business owner whose operation suffered revenue or cash flow losses due to the Eaton Fire evacuation and disruption — but had no physical property damage — wants to know whether SBA assistance is available.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes. The SBA offers Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDLs) in addition to physical damage loans. EIDLs are specifically designed for businesses, private nonprofit organizations, and agricultural enterprises that have suffered substantial economic injury — meaning a significant loss of revenue or working capital — as a result of a declared disaster, even if the business had no physical property damage. EIDLs provide working capital to help businesses meet ordinary and necessary financial obligations that cannot be met as a result of the disaster. The maximum EIDL amount is up to $2 million (subject to creditworthiness and demonstrated need). Apply online at lending.sba.gov, call 1-800-659-2955 (TTY 1-800-877-8339), or visit an SBA Disaster Loan Outreach Center. The deadline to apply for EIDLs related to the Eaton Fire is March 31, 2025. SBA encourages applications even if the business owner is unsure they need the loan, as applying establishes eligibility for other assistance programs.

question_text: I've been displaced and I'm worried about missing important mail — FEMA letters, insurance documents, bills. What should I do?
official_question: I've been displaced and I'm worried about missing important mail — FEMA letters, insurance documents, bills. What should I do?
normalized_resident_need: A displaced resident wants to make sure they receive critical mail — including FEMA correspondence, insurance documents, and bills — while living at a temporary address.

source_answer.official_answer: Immediately set up a mail forward with USPS to ensure all mail is redirected to your current temporary address. You can do this online at usps.com (search for 'mail forwarding' or 'change of address'), by visiting any post office, or by calling 1-800-275-8777. USPS mail forwarding is free for the first 12 months. Critically, update your address with FEMA at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362, as FEMA determination letters and disaster checks are sent by mail and will not be forwarded. Also update your address with: your bank and creditors; the Social Security Administration (1-800-772-1213 or ssa.gov); your insurance companies; the IRS (using Form 8822, or through your next tax return); your employer; your health insurance provider; and any schools your children attend. Keep a record of every organization you've notified. If you expect to move again before permanently resettling, notify FEMA and USPS each time your address changes.

source_answer.official_answer: Immediately set up a mail forward with USPS to ensure all mail is redirected to your current temporary address. You can do this online at usps.com (search for 'mail forwarding' or 'change of address'), by visiting any post office, or by calling 1-800-275-8777. USPS mail forwarding is free for the first 12 months. Critically, update your address with FEMA at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362, as FEMA determination letters and disaster checks are sent by mail and will not be forwarded. Also update your address with: your bank and creditors; the Social Security Administration (1-800-772-1213 or ssa.gov); your insurance companies; the IRS (using Form 8822, or through your next tax return); your employer; your health insurance provider; and any schools your children attend. Keep a record of every organization you've notified. If you expect to move again before permanently resettling, notify FEMA and USPS each time your address changes.

question_text: I have horses and goats. Where can I take them to evacuate?
official_question: I have horses and goats. Where can I take them to evacuate?
normalized_resident_need: A resident with horses, goats, or other large animals affected by the Eaton Fire needs to know how to evacuate the animals, where to take them, and how to get help if they cannot reach their animals.

source_answer.official_answer: For assistance evacuating animals or locating emergency animal shelters for livestock and large animals, call the LA County Department of Animal Care and Control at (562) 940-6898. This line handles large animal evacuation coordination and can direct you to appropriate emergency facilities. During the Eaton Fire response, equestrian facilities and fairgrounds in the region were used as emergency large-animal shelters; call the hotline for current open locations. Comprehensive information on local shelters for people, pets, and animals is also available at lacounty.gov/emergency. The Pasadena Humane Society also assisted with animal evacuations during the Eaton Fire response; contact them at (626) 792-7151. For animals still on fire-affected properties that owners cannot reach, contact the Department of Animal Care and Control to arrange for animal welfare checks and emergency feeding if needed. When returning to your property, assess any injured animals and contact a veterinarian or the Humane Society for assistance with injured livestock.

question_text: How do I know when the air outside is safe? What AQI number should I be watching for?
official_question: How do I know when the air outside is safe? What AQI number should I be watching for?
normalized_resident_need: A resident wants to know how to check current air quality conditions and understand what AQI values mean for their safety and outdoor activities.

source_answer.official_answer: The Air Quality Index (AQI) is the standard measure of outdoor air quality. You can monitor current AQI for your specific location at AirNow.gov, through the South Coast Air Quality Management District at aqmd.gov, or through smartphone apps such as IQAir or PurpleAir. AQI levels and their general health implications are: 0–50 (Good — little or no risk); 51–100 (Moderate — acceptable for most, but unusually sensitive people should reduce prolonged outdoor exertion); 101–150 (Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups — children, older adults, and people with heart or lung disease should limit prolonged outdoor exertion); 151–200 (Unhealthy — everyone should limit prolonged outdoor exertion; sensitive groups should avoid outdoor exertion); 201–300 (Very Unhealthy — everyone should avoid outdoor exertion); 301+ (Hazardous — everyone should remain indoors and avoid all outdoor exertion). During active debris removal operations, local air quality may be temporarily worse than area-wide AQI readings suggest — check for any local advisories from LA County Public Health in addition to the AQI. When air quality is in the 'Unhealthy' range or above, keep doors and windows closed and use HEPA air purifiers indoors.
required_answer_elements: Direct the user to AirNow.gov or aqmd.gov to check current AQI.
Provide the AQI scale with health guidance for each level: 0–50 Good, 51–100 Moderate, 101–150 USG, 151–200 Unhealthy, 201–300 Very Unhealthy, 301+ Hazardous.
Note that local air quality during debris removal may be temporarily worse than area-wide readings.
Advise keeping windows and doors closed and using HEPA purifiers when AQI is unhealthy or above.

Stating that any AQI level is completely safe for all individuals (sensitive groups have lower thresholds).

question_text: How do I protect my young children from the smoke and ash? Are they more at risk than adults?
official_question: How do I protect my young children from the smoke and ash? Are they more at risk than adults?
normalized_resident_need: A parent wants to know how to protect their young children from wildfire smoke and ash exposure and whether children face greater risks than adults.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes — children are at higher risk from wildfire smoke and ash than healthy adults for several reasons: their lungs and immune systems are still developing; they breathe more air relative to their body weight; they are closer to the ground where ash and dust accumulate; and they are more likely to put their hands or objects in their mouths. Take the following precautions for children. Keep children indoors as much as possible when outdoor air quality is poor, during debris removal operations, and during windy conditions that stir up ash. Do not allow children to play in ash-covered outdoor areas. Use HEPA air purifiers in rooms where children sleep and spend time. If children must go outside, N95 masks in child-specific sizes can provide some protection, though small children may not tolerate them. Keep children and pets away from ash-covered areas and objects. Wash children's hands and exposed skin frequently and before eating. Watch for respiratory symptoms including coughing, wheezing, fast breathing, or shortness of breath — if symptoms are concerning or persistent, consult a pediatrician. Children, pregnant individuals, and pets should avoid fire-affected areas entirely until Phase 1 and Phase 2 hazardous material removal are completed.
required_answer_elements: Confirm that children face higher risk than healthy adults due to developing lungs, higher breathing rates, and proximity to the ground.
Recommend keeping children indoors during poor air quality, debris removal, and windy conditions.
Advise against allowing children to play in ash-covered areas.
State that children should avoid fire-affected areas until Phase 1 and Phase 2 debris removal are completed.
Recommend consulting a pediatrician if respiratory symptoms appear.
forbidden_claims: Telling the user children and adults face equal risk from wildfire smoke.
Recommending specific medications for children.
Stating that standard surgical or cloth masks adequately protect children (N95 in child-appropriate sizes is the recommended option).
Guaranteeing any measure eliminates all risk to children.

question_text: I've swept up piles of ash inside my house. How do I dispose of it safely?
official_question: I've swept up piles of ash inside my house. How do I dispose of it safely?
normalized_resident_need: A resident who has been cleaning ash and soot from their home wants to know how to safely bag and dispose of the collected material.

source_answer.official_answer: Ash and soot from wildfire cleanup should be handled with caution because they may contain hazardous particles including heavy metals and traces of asbestos from burned building materials. When disposing of ash collected during indoor or outdoor cleanup: seal ash and soot in heavy-duty plastic bags, double-bagging if possible, to minimize the release of particles during handling and transport. Label the bags clearly. Place sealed bags in covered trash bins to prevent them from being disturbed by wind or animals. Do not place ash in green waste bins or recycling — place it in regular household trash. Do not dump ash down storm drains, as this harms waterways and aquatic environments. For driveways and walkways, hose down the area with water before sweeping to minimize airborne particles, and dispose of the collected ash in sealed bags rather than washing it into storm drains. For large quantities of ash and debris from destroyed structures, do not attempt to dispose of this yourself — it must be handled through the Phase 1 and Phase 2 debris removal programs (see DEBRIS_PHASES_001).

question_text: I lost all my financial documents — account numbers, statements, everything. How do I access my money and accounts?
official_question: I lost all my financial documents — account numbers, statements, everything. How do I access my money and accounts?
normalized_resident_need: A resident who lost physical financial documents (bank account information, statements, checks) in the fire wants to know how to regain access to their accounts and protect against identity theft.

source_answer.official_answer: You can regain access to your bank accounts and financial records even without physical documents. Contact your bank or credit union directly — bring any identification you have (or explain that your ID was also lost in the fire). Most financial institutions can verify your identity through other means, such as your Social Security number, date of birth, and answers to security questions, and can issue replacement cards and statements. Many banks have disaster relief policies that include waiving replacement card fees, providing emergency cash advances, or extending loan payment due dates for disaster-affected customers — ask your banker specifically about disaster relief options. If you suspect that your personal financial information may have been compromised or stolen due to the fire or evacuation, place a fraud alert or credit freeze with the three major credit bureaus: Equifax (equifax.com), Experian (experian.com), and TransUnion (transunion.com). Freezes are free and prevent new credit from being opened in your name. You can also obtain free copies of your credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com to check for unauthorized activity. For questions about FDIC insurance protecting your deposits, call 1-877-275-3342 or visit fdic.gov. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) also provides disaster-related guidance at consumerfinance.gov.

question_text: I want to help Eaton Fire victims. What's the best way to donate or volunteer?
official_question: I want to help Eaton Fire victims. What's the best way to donate or volunteer?
normalized_resident_need: A person who was not affected by the fire wants to help Eaton Fire survivors and wants to know how to donate money or goods effectively, and how to volunteer without causing harm.

source_answer.official_answer: To donate: give to established, vetted organizations working in the Eaton Fire recovery rather than to individuals or unverified crowdfunding campaigns. You can verify a charity's legitimacy at give.org (BBB Wise Giving Alliance), charitynavigator.org, or by checking 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status at apps.irs.gov/app/eos. Organizations active in the Eaton Fire response include the American Red Cross (redcross.org), United Way of Greater Los Angeles (unitedwayla.org), and World Central Kitchen (wck.org). Monetary donations are almost always more efficient than material goods donations, which create sorting and warehousing costs. If donating goods, contact the receiving organization first to confirm they are accepting that type of donation. To volunteer: do not self-deploy to disaster areas without coordination — unsolicited volunteers can interfere with professional response operations and put themselves at risk. Register as a volunteer through the LA County Volunteer Portal at lacounty.gov/volunteers, through the American Red Cross, or through 211 LA, which coordinates volunteer opportunities with vetted organizations. For debris cleanup specifically, wait for official coordination before entering fire-affected areas.

question_text: Where do I go to get help starting the permit process for my rebuild?
official_question: Where do I go to get help starting the permit process for my rebuild?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner is ready to start the permit process to rebuild after the Eaton Fire and wants to know where to go and what help is available in person.

source_answer.official_answer: LA County has established One-Stop Permit Centers specifically for residents impacted by the Palisades and Eaton fires in unincorporated LA County communities. Walk-in visits are welcome and consultation appointments can also be scheduled at the Altadena and Calabasas One-Stop Permit Centers. At a One-Stop Permit Center, representatives from multiple LA County permitting agencies are available — including the Fire Department, Regional Planning, Public Health, and Public Works Building and Safety — to guide property owners and their representatives through the rebuild process and answer questions. Homeowners are provided with a packet containing information specific to their property, including permit records, assessor records, and property attributes. To find current hours and locations or to schedule an appointment, visit recovery.lacounty.gov/rebuilding/one-stop-permit-centers or email recovery@planning.lacounty.gov.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes. Eaton Fire rebuild projects must comply with current Building Code requirements, which include the installation of fire sprinklers. question_text: Can I replace my burned home with a manufactured or modular home instead of traditional construction?
official_question: Can I replace my burned home with a manufactured or modular home instead of traditional construction?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner wants to know whether they can rebuild using a manufactured or modular/prefab home instead of conventional stick-frame construction.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes, manufactured housing and factory-built (modular) housing are permitted as permanent replacement structures in the Eaton Fire area, subject to requirements. Manufactured housing registration is overseen by the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD). LA County issues permits and inspects units being placed on private property. If the property is in the Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone, LA County requires documentation confirming the unit meets fire-resistant construction requirements before issuing a permit — look for an insignia or label affixed to the unit indicating it has been approved. For permanent use, manufactured homes must be installed on a foundation system consisting of a continuous concrete footing. LA County inspects utility connections for code compliance. Factory-built (modular) housing is also overseen by HCD under a separate program. Contact LA County Building and Safety at your local One-Stop Permit Center and HCD at hcd.ca.gov for guidance on your specific unit and site.

question_text: Does my rebuild project require a soils report? How do I know?
official_question: Does my rebuild project require a soils report? How do I know?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner planning to rebuild wants to know whether they need to commission a geotechnical or soils report before they can get a building permit.

source_answer.official_answer: Not necessarily. If your foundation is a conventional raised or slab-on-grade with continuous footings designed to meet specified minimum standards, a soils report is generally not required. Soils reports are still required in certain circumstances, including: foundations using caissons or deep piles; sites with identified geotechnical hazards such as liquefaction, landslide, or expansive soils; projects involving basement walls; and certain other criteria as determined by the plan check engineer. Additionally, LA County Public Works Geotechnical and Materials Engineering approval may be required before rebuilding on a property where a known geologic hazard is present — this is particularly relevant in hilly areas of the Eaton Fire burn zone where slope stability may be a concern after debris removal. Ask your assigned land use planner or the Building and Safety plan check engineer at the One-Stop Permit Center whether a soils report is required for your specific site.

question_text: What plans and documents do I actually need to bring in to start the permit process?
official_question: What plans and documents do I actually need to bring in to start the permit process?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner is ready to start the permitting process and wants to know exactly what documents and plans to bring to the first submission.

source_answer.official_answer: To begin the permit review process with LA County, you need only one application with architectural plans — specifically a site plan, floor plan, and elevations — along with property ownership information. You do not need full structural plans at the start. After LA County staff reviews your submission to determine whether it qualifies as a like-for-like rebuild, identifies any additional requirements, and finalizes the project scope, they may ask for additional materials to complete the zoning review. Once LA County issues a zoning clearance and you want to move forward to the building permit stage, you will need to submit: structural plans, structural calculations by a licensed architect or engineer (unless the project uses prescriptive construction), and energy plans. You will not need to file a separate application at that stage — staff will notify you when these additional plans are required. For the full list of requirements, refer to the Eaton and Palisades Fire Rebuild Minimum Residential Submittal Requirements document available at LA County Building and Safety (dpw.lacounty.gov). Plans can be submitted now; construction cannot begin until debris removal is complete and a permit is issued.

question_text: Do I need to hire a surveyor to mark my property lines before I can rebuild?
official_question: Do I need to hire a surveyor to mark my property lines before I can rebuild?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner planning to rebuild wants to know whether they need to hire a surveyor to locate their property lines before construction can begin.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes, for most rebuild projects. Prior to the start of construction, a corner record survey identifying the property boundaries is required for most Eaton Fire rebuilds. It is the property owner's responsibility to hire a licensed private land surveyor to mark the property lines. A survey is necessary to verify setbacks and ensure the new structure is placed correctly on the lot — this is particularly important in cases where property lines may have been obscured by the fire or where original structures were built near property boundaries. Budget for survey costs early in your rebuild planning, as the survey must typically be completed before construction begins. normalized_resident_need: A property owner whose home was destroyed wants to know how LA County will determine the original square footage of their home for the purposes of like-for-like rebuild eligibility.

source_answer.official_answer: LA County determines the square footage of a destroyed property by reviewing all available records and evidence. Sources reviewed may include: previous land use and zoning approvals; building permit records on file with LA County; Coastal Commission records (if applicable); County Assessor's Office records; and photographs. Recently issued permits for new homes or ADUs from the 2020 or 2023 code cycle may also be reissued without full plan review, which can accelerate the process if the homeowner had recent permitted work. If you have your own records — such as prior appraisals, tax records, prior real estate listings, photos, or old permit documents — bring them to your One-Stop Permit Center consultation. The square footage determination affects whether your project qualifies as a like-for-like rebuild and what zoning exemptions apply.

question_text: Do I need a temporary power pole on my lot to start rebuilding? How do I get one?
official_question: Do I need a temporary power pole on my lot to start rebuilding? How do I get one?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner beginning a rebuild in Altadena wants to know whether they need a temporary power pole and how to obtain one.

source_answer.official_answer: Most homeowners rebuilding in Altadena will need a temporary power pole if: the original power service was removed or destroyed in the fire; the project involves a full rebuild or new construction; or the site needs temporary power for pool maintenance or security purposes. If your existing electrical service is still active and usable, you may not need a temporary power pole. The step-by-step process to obtain a temporary power pole is: (1) Contact Southern California Edison (SCE) to obtain location approval and set up an account with them. (2) Apply for an electrical permit with LA County Building and Safety. (3) Hire a qualified electrician (or act as owner-builder) to install the temporary power pole in compliance with code. (4) Schedule and pass a LA County inspection. (5) LA County's inspector submits a release to SCE for connection. (6) Request service connection from SCE. (7) Power is connected and turned on. For additional technical details, refer to the Electrical Service Requirements document available from LA County Public Works. Contact the One-Stop Permit Center for assistance.

question_text: My house burned down but my pool survived. What are my obligations for pool safety while I'm rebuilding?
official_question: My house burned down but my pool survived. What are my obligations for pool safety while I'm rebuilding?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner whose home was destroyed but whose pool survived wants to know their obligations for pool fencing and safety, and whether they need to drain the pool.

source_answer.official_answer: Swimming pools and spas in LA County are required at all times to be surrounded by a 5-foot-high fence or barrier. If the home and/or garage was part of the pool barrier and was destroyed in the fire, temporary fencing must be installed immediately. A permit is not required to install a temporary pool fence. Acceptable temporary chain-link fencing must be 11-gauge with openings no more than 1¾ inches measured horizontally. Regarding pool drainage: draining a pool is generally not recommended. If damage requires draining, residents in unincorporated areas may drain freshwater pools (not saltwater) to the sewer, but only if a three-inch P-trap is legally installed with a sewer permit. Draining directly into manholes is not allowed. Pool owners should skim and filter pool water before draining to reduce solids discharged. Do not drain pools during or within 24 hours after active rainfall. If the pool is within the ash footprint and you opt into the government debris removal program, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers will remove fire debris from the pool but will not refill or remove the pool. For comprehensive pool health and safety guidance after a fire, see ph.lacounty.gov/eh/safety/returning-home-after-fire.htm.

question_text: I'm thinking about selling my burned lot. What rebuild rights go to the new buyer?
official_question: I'm thinking about selling my burned lot. What rebuild rights go to the new buyer?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner considering selling their fire-damaged lot wants to understand what rebuild benefits and rights transfer to a buyer versus remain exclusive to the original owner.

source_answer.official_answer: If a fire-damaged lot is sold, the buyer's eligibility for certain recovery programs depends on the specific benefit. Expedited permitting: expedited permitting for fire rebuilds is available to everyone — including buyers — within two years of the start of the emergency declaration (January 7, 2025), regardless of whether the property has changed hands. Applications for like-for-like rebuild projects must be submitted to Regional Planning within this two-year window; the Director of Regional Planning can grant up to three one-year extensions if needed. Temporary housing on-site: buyers are not eligible for the temporary housing program (RV/mobile home on the lot), which requires evidence that the applicant lived at the property within the past 12 months. Like-for-like setback rights: if a buyer does not use the original building footprint, they will be required to comply with new Community Standards District setback requirements and other current zoning regulations. The like-for-like setback and zoning exemptions are strongest when the original footprint is preserved. Sellers and buyers should consult LA County Regional Planning at planning.lacounty.gov about the specific rights transferring with any particular property transaction.

question_text: My business had to close because of the fire. Does my insurance cover lost income?
official_question: My business had to close because of the fire. Does my insurance cover lost income?
normalized_resident_need: A business owner whose operations were interrupted by the Eaton Fire wants to know whether business interruption insurance applies and how to file a claim.

source_answer.official_answer: Business interruption insurance (also called business income insurance or loss of business income coverage) is designed to replace income and cover ongoing fixed expenses when a business must temporarily close due to a covered disaster. Coverage typically pays for: lost net income that the business would have earned; continuing operating expenses such as rent, utilities, and loan payments; and sometimes additional expenses incurred to minimize the interruption (e.g., renting temporary space). Key steps for filing a business interruption claim: Notify your insurer immediately. Gather and preserve documentation of your pre-loss income — including tax returns, profit and loss statements, and payroll records — as the insurer will use these to calculate your loss. Document all ongoing expenses you are still paying despite the closure. Keep records of any extra expenses you incur to keep operations running. Review your policy carefully for the waiting period (typically 24–72 hours before coverage begins), the coverage period limit, and any sublimits. If your business interruption coverage is denied or disputed, contact the California Department of Insurance at 1-800-927-4357 or file a complaint at insurance.ca.gov.

question_text: My insurance company sent an adjuster but I don't think the offer is fair. What are my options?
official_question: My insurance company sent an adjuster but I don't think the offer is fair. What are my options?
normalized_resident_need: A homeowner believes their insurance settlement offer is too low and wants to know how to challenge it and whether hiring a public adjuster is worthwhile.

source_answer.official_answer: After a disaster, your insurance company will send a claims adjuster to assess your damage and estimate the cost to repair or rebuild. This adjuster works for the insurance company. If you believe the estimate is too low or the settlement offer is unfair, you have several options. First, get independent contractor estimates and compare them with the adjuster's assessment. You can submit a written request for reconsideration with supporting documentation. You may also hire a licensed public adjuster — a professional who represents the policyholder (not the insurer) to negotiate the claim on your behalf. Public adjusters typically charge a percentage of the claim settlement (commonly 10–15%); under California law, fees for public adjusters on residential property claims cannot exceed certain limits. Verify that any public adjuster you hire is licensed by the California Department of Insurance: check at insurance.ca.gov. If your claim remains disputed, you can request mediation through the CDI's mediation program, or file a formal complaint with the CDI at 1-800-927-4357 or insurance.ca.gov. You may also consult a licensed attorney specializing in insurance disputes.

source_answer.official_answer: If your insurance company is not responding within a reasonable time, is denying claims you believe are covered, or is otherwise acting in bad faith, the California Department of Insurance (CDI) is the agency that regulates insurance companies and can intervene. Here's how to escalate. Step 1: Document everything. Keep a written log (claim diary) of all calls, emails, and correspondence, including dates and names of everyone you spoke with. Step 2: Contact your insurer in writing. Send a formal written complaint to your insurer and request a written response. Step 3: File a complaint with the CDI. For disputed residential claims, the CDI offers a free, non-binding mediation program that can resolve disputes without litigation. Step 5: Consult a licensed attorney. If CDI mediation does not resolve the dispute, an attorney specializing in insurance bad faith may be warranted. question_text: I'm a contractor employee doing ash cleanup. What protections am I entitled to on the job?
official_question: I'm a contractor employee doing ash cleanup. What protections am I entitled to on the job?
normalized_resident_need: A worker hired to clean up ash or debris from the Eaton Fire wants to know what safety protections their employer is required to provide and how to report unsafe conditions.

source_answer.official_answer: Workers performing wildfire cleanup and debris removal are entitled to workplace safety protections under California law and Cal/OSHA regulations. Employers must: provide appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) at no cost to workers, including properly fitted N95 or P-100 respirators, safety goggles, gloves, Tyvek suits, and sturdy closed-toe footwear; train workers on the hazards present in wildfire ash and debris, including asbestos, heavy metals, and other toxic substances; ensure workers take regular rest breaks in clean areas away from contaminated zones; and provide washing facilities for handwashing and decontamination. Workers have the right to refuse work they believe presents an imminent danger to their health or safety. If you believe your employer is not providing required safety protections, you may file a confidential complaint with Cal/OSHA at the California Department of Industrial Relations: dir.ca.gov/dosh or by calling 1-800-963-9424. Workers with symptoms related to ash or smoke exposure should report them to their employer and seek medical attention. If you are injured or become ill as a result of cleanup work, you may be entitled to workers' compensation benefits.

question_text: I'm a veteran. Are there any special programs that can help me after the fire?
official_question: I'm a veteran. Are there any special programs that can help me after the fire?
normalized_resident_need: A veteran affected by the Eaton Fire wants to know what veteran-specific assistance programs are available in addition to general disaster programs.

source_answer.official_answer: Veterans affected by the Eaton Fire may be eligible for both general disaster assistance programs and veteran-specific support. General assistance: All veterans should apply for FEMA Individual Assistance (DisasterAssistance.gov or 1-800-621-3362) and SBA disaster loans (lending.sba.gov or 1-800-659-2955), as these programs are available to all residents. VA-specific assistance: If your primary residence is a VA-guaranteed home loan property, contact your VA loan servicer immediately about forbearance and foreclosure prevention options. The VA has issued guidance encouraging servicers to provide payment relief for disaster-affected VA borrowers. Contact the VA home loan assistance line at 1-877-827-3702. For veterans with service-connected disabilities whose adapted housing was damaged, the VA's Specially Adapted Housing (SAH) grant program may provide assistance with rebuilding or modifying a home — contact your VA regional office or visit va.gov/housing-assistance/adaptive-housing-grants. The LA County Department of Military and Veterans Affairs (DMVA) has representatives available at Disaster Recovery Centers and can connect veterans with additional resources: call 1-800-500-0572 or visit va.lacounty.gov.

question_text: I'm displaced and I need childcare while I'm trying to deal with all of this. Where can I find help?
official_question: I'm displaced and I need childcare while I'm trying to deal with all of this. Where can I find help?
normalized_resident_need: A parent displaced by the Eaton Fire needs childcare while managing displacement, recovery, and work, and wants to know where to find emergency childcare assistance.

source_answer.official_answer: Finding childcare while displaced can be challenging, but several resources exist. Start by calling 211 (or visiting 211la.org), which can connect you with local childcare referral agencies that maintain up-to-date listings of available licensed providers in your current area. The Child Care Resource Center (CCRC) and the Crystal Stairs Child Care Resource and Referral agency serve different parts of LA County and can help match families with available childcare slots and emergency financial assistance for childcare costs — reach the referral system at childrenshome.org or through 211. Subsidized childcare through California's subsidized childcare programs (CalWORKs Stage 1, 2, and 3, and the Alternative Payment Program) may be available for income-qualifying families; contact your local DPSS office or call 1-866-613-3777. Head Start and Early Head Start programs serve income-eligible children from birth through age five and may have openings — contact the Los Angeles County Office of Education at lacoe.edu. FEMA Individual Assistance may include some childcare-related expenses as a component of disaster-related needs — document all childcare costs you incur during displacement. Disaster Recovery Centers also have representatives from the Department of Children and Family Services who can assist with connecting families to services.

official_question: I'm undocumented and can't apply for FEMA. What help is available to me?
normalized_resident_need: An undocumented resident affected by the Eaton Fire who is not eligible for FEMA or other federal programs wants to know what disaster assistance is available to them.

source_answer.official_answer: Undocumented residents who are not eligible for FEMA Individual Assistance or other federal programs have access to several non-federal resources after the Eaton Fire. Emergency food: The Los Angeles Regional Food Bank (lafoodbank.org) and World Central Kitchen hot-meal sites serve all residents regardless of immigration status — no documentation required. Contact 211 for current food distribution locations. Emergency shelter: 211 LA (2-1-1 or 211la.org) can connect residents with emergency housing resources that do not require documentation. Some faith-based and nonprofit shelters serve all residents regardless of status. Nonprofit financial assistance: The United Way of Greater Los Angeles (unitedwayla.org) and other disaster relief funds provide assistance to undocumented residents. The California Disaster Assistance Fund and the California Disaster Relief Fund may also provide support to undocumented individuals — contact 211 for current programs. Mental health: The SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline (1-800-985-5990) and the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline are available to all callers regardless of immigration status. Medical care: Community health centers (Federally Qualified Health Centers) are required to serve patients regardless of immigration status and on a sliding fee scale — find one at findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov. Remember: emergency disaster aid such as food, shelter, medical assistance, and temporary financial support is not counted as 'public charge' and will not affect future immigration applications.

question_text: My car was destroyed in the fire. Does my car insurance cover this?
official_question: My car was destroyed in the fire. Does my car insurance cover this?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose vehicle was destroyed or damaged by the Eaton Fire wants to know whether their auto insurance covers the loss and how to file a claim.

source_answer.official_answer: Vehicle damage from wildfire is typically covered under the comprehensive portion of an auto insurance policy, not the collision portion. If you have comprehensive coverage on your vehicle, it should cover damage or total loss caused by fire, smoke, and ash. If your vehicle was only carrying liability coverage (the minimum required by California law), fire damage to your vehicle would generally not be covered under your auto policy. To file a claim: contact your auto insurance company as soon as possible. If your vehicle was in a location you cannot access due to evacuation orders, tell your insurer — documentation of the vehicle's loss may be possible even without immediate physical access. If your vehicle is totaled, your insurer will pay the actual cash value (ACV) of the vehicle at the time of loss, minus your deductible. If you disagree with the ACV assessment, you can request a re-evaluation and provide evidence of comparable vehicles' market value. Rental car coverage (if you have it on your policy) may help cover a replacement vehicle while your claim is being processed. File your claim promptly, as some policies have filing deadlines. If you have questions about your coverage or a claim dispute, contact the California Department of Insurance at 1-800-927-4357.

question_text: I lost all my medical records and prescription bottles in the fire. How do I get my medications and medical history back?
official_question: I lost all my medical records and prescription bottles in the fire. How do I get my medications and medical history back?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose medical records and prescription bottles were lost in the Eaton Fire wants to know how to regain access to medications and their medical history.

source_answer.official_answer: Replacing medical records and accessing medications after a disaster is often easier than residents expect. For prescription medications: contact your pharmacy directly — pharmacies maintain electronic records of your prescription history and can typically fill emergency supplies of most medications even without a physical prescription bottle. In California, pharmacists may provide emergency supplies of certain ongoing medications without a new prescription in a declared emergency. If your regular pharmacy is inaccessible, most major pharmacy chains can access your records at any of their locations statewide. For controlled substances, there are stricter rules — ask your pharmacist what documentation is needed. The Emergency Prescription Assistance Program (EPAP) through FEMA may also help uninsured individuals access prescription medications — ask at a Disaster Recovery Center. For medical records: contact your doctors, hospitals, and health systems directly and request copies of your records. Under federal HIPAA law, healthcare providers must give you access to your records, typically within 30 days. Many health systems now have patient portals (such as MyChart) where you can access your own medical records electronically without waiting for paper copies. If you are managing a serious or complex medical condition and need help coordinating care after displacement, the Eaton Health Village in Pasadena (Mondays and Wednesdays) provides free medical services — contact 211 for current hours.

source_answer.official_answer: Replacing medical records and accessing medications after a disaster is often easier than residents expect. For prescription medications: contact your pharmacy directly — pharmacies maintain electronic records of your prescription history and can typically fill emergency supplies of most medications even without a physical prescription bottle. In California, pharmacists may provide emergency supplies of certain ongoing medications without a new prescription in a declared emergency. If your regular pharmacy is inaccessible, most major pharmacy chains can access your records at any of their locations statewide. For controlled substances, there are stricter rules — ask your pharmacist what documentation is needed. The Emergency Prescription Assistance Program (EPAP) through FEMA may also help uninsured individuals access prescription medications — ask at a Disaster Recovery Center. For medical records: contact your doctors, hospitals, and health systems directly and request copies of your records. Under federal HIPAA law, healthcare providers must give you access to your records, typically within 30 days. Many health systems now have patient portals (such as MyChart) where you can access your own medical records electronically without waiting for paper copies. question_text: A contractor took my deposit and did nothing, and my landlord won't return my security deposit. Can I take them to small claims court?
official_question: A contractor took my deposit and did nothing, and my landlord won't return my security deposit. Can I take them to small claims court?
normalized_resident_need: A disaster survivor who has been wronged by a contractor or landlord wants to know whether small claims court is a viable option and how to use it.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes. California Small Claims Court is a low-cost, simplified court process designed for disputes involving money — and is often appropriate for contractor and landlord-tenant disputes arising from the Eaton Fire. In small claims court, you represent yourself (no lawyer required, though you can consult one beforehand), and the process is designed to be accessible without legal training. Key small claims limits and rules: individuals can sue for up to $12,500 in small claims court; businesses can sue for up to $6,250. You must file in the court of the county where the defendant lives or does business. The filing fee is typically $30–$100 depending on the amount of the claim. Common Eaton Fire-related small claims cases include: contractor took a deposit and did not perform work; landlord failed to return a security deposit within 21 days; landlord made illegal deductions from a security deposit; and contractor performed substandard work. Before filing, consider first submitting a demand letter to the other party, which is a written notice of your claim and the amount owed — this often results in resolution without court. For free help preparing a small claims case, contact the LA County Department of Consumer and Business Affairs at (800) 593-8222 or dcba.lacounty.gov. The Los Angeles Superior Court small claims self-help center at lacourt.org also provides guidance.

question_text: I own rental property that burned down. What are my insurance, tenant, and rebuild obligations?
official_question: I own rental property that burned down. What are my insurance, tenant, and rebuild obligations?
normalized_resident_need: A rental property owner whose building was destroyed or damaged by the Eaton Fire wants to understand their insurance, tenant, and rebuild obligations.

source_answer.official_answer: Rental property owners affected by the Eaton Fire have obligations and rights across several areas. Insurance: Your landlord insurance policy (also called a dwelling fire policy or rental dwelling policy) should cover the structure itself and potentially lost rental income during the period the property is uninhabitable. File your claim promptly and document all damage before cleanup begins. Loss of Rents coverage (if included) compensates you for rental income lost while the property is being repaired or rebuilt. Tenant rights: If your rental unit was destroyed or made substantially uninhabitable, your tenants have the right to terminate their leases without penalty under California Civil Code Section 1932. You must return security deposits within 21 days of the tenant vacating — you cannot deduct fire damage caused by the disaster from the deposit. You cannot charge rent for periods when the unit is uninhabitable. Price gouging protections prohibit raising rents on replacement units by more than 10% during the state of emergency. Rebuilding: Rental property owners rebuilding multi-unit structures should work with LA County Regional Planning; like-for-like zoning exemptions may apply. Apply for FEMA Individual Assistance even as a landlord — renters can apply on their own behalf, and your structure losses may qualify for SBA disaster loans (up to $500,000 for primary residences, or the business loan program for rental properties). For guidance, contact the LA County Department of Consumer and Business Affairs at (800) 593-8222.
required_answer_elements: State that landlord insurance (dwelling fire/rental dwelling policy) covers the structure and may include Loss of Rents coverage.
State that tenants can legally terminate leases without penalty if the unit is uninhabitable (Civil Code §1932).
State that landlords cannot deduct fire damage from security deposits and must return deposits within 21 days.
State that price gouging rules prohibit raising rents on replacement units by more than 10% during the emergency.

Telling landlords they can continue charging rent for uninhabitable units.

question_text: My property drains onto my neighbor's lot. Will I need to fix this when I rebuild?
official_question: My property drains onto my neighbor's lot. Will I need to fix this when I rebuild?
normalized_resident_need: A property owner planning to rebuild wants to know whether their rebuild project must address existing cross-lot drainage onto a neighboring property.

source_answer.official_answer: Cross-lot drainage — where stormwater runoff from one property flows onto an adjacent property — must be addressed as part of the rebuild permit process. There are two compliance options. Option 1: Mitigate on-site. Any drainage impact on an adjacent property must be fully mitigated on your own property so that runoff no longer crosses onto the neighbor's lot. This may require grading changes, retention systems, or other drainage improvements. Option 2: Offsite drainage covenant. If on-site mitigation is not practicable, the adjacent property owner must sign and record a drainage acceptance covenant consenting to receive the runoff. This covenant runs with the land and is a permanent recorded document. A third path exists if the impact is negligible: if your architect or engineer of record determines that the pre- and post-construction net drainage effect at the property line is negligible, that determination must be documented on the building plans as a permanent statement. Contact LA County Public Works or your engineer for site-specific drainage analysis and plan requirements.
required_answer_elements: State that cross-lot drainage must be addressed: either mitigated on-site or resolved through a recorded drainage acceptance covenant with the adjacent property owner.
Mention the negligible-impact exception: an engineer of record can certify negligible impact on the plans.
Direct the user to LA County Public Works or their project engineer for site-specific analysis.
forbidden_claims: Telling the user cross-lot drainage does not need to be addressed for like-for-like rebuilds.
Telling the user a drainage covenant is always possible without the neighbor's consent.
Inventing specific drainage mitigation design requirements.
Promising that all drainage impacts will be classified as negligible.

question_text: English isn't my first language. Are disaster resources available in Spanish and other languages?
official_question: English isn't my first language. Are disaster resources available in Spanish and other languages?
normalized_resident_need: A resident whose primary language is not English wants to know how to access disaster recovery programs and resources in their own language.

source_answer.official_answer: Yes. Disaster recovery resources for the Eaton Fire are available in many languages. FEMA Individual Assistance: FEMA's helpline at 1-800-621-3362 offers translation services for over 100 languages. The DisasterAssistance.gov website is also available in Spanish and other languages through the browser translation function. The FEMA mobile app supports multiple languages. 211 LA: Calling 2-1-1 connects residents with operators who speak multiple languages, including Spanish, Mandarin, Cantonese, Korean, Armenian, and others. Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA): The California EDD fire-dedicated phone lines include English (1-833-998-2284), Spanish (1-855-964-0634), and other languages (1-800-300-5616). SBA disaster loans: SBA staff at Disaster Loan Outreach Centers can assist in multiple languages. At Disaster Recovery Centers: Representatives from LA County's Office of Immigrant Affairs and multilingual staff from various agencies are on-site. question_text: I can't find any rental housing — there's nothing available in my area. Can FEMA provide a trailer or manufactured unit?
official_question: I can't find any rental housing — there's nothing available in my area. Can FEMA provide a trailer or manufactured unit?
normalized_resident_need: A displaced resident cannot find rental housing because the local rental market is overwhelmed and wants to know if FEMA can provide a temporary trailer or manufactured unit.

source_answer.official_answer: FEMA's Direct Housing Assistance program provides temporary housing units — including manufactured housing units (trailers) or recreational vehicles — to eligible disaster survivors who cannot find rental housing in the affected area. This program is distinct from FEMA's standard rental assistance grant (which provides funds for you to rent housing yourself). Direct Housing is typically activated when FEMA determines that adequate rental housing is not available in the disaster area. To be considered for Direct Housing: you must first apply for and be found eligible for FEMA Individual Assistance; your case must be identified as one where rental housing is unavailable or inaccessible; and you must be able to have a unit sited on your lot or at a group site. Manufactured housing units placed on your lot require proof of utility connections and lot suitability. Direct Housing is temporary and typically provided for 18 months, with possible extensions. FEMA notifies eligible survivors of Direct Housing availability; you cannot self-select it at the time of application. Contact FEMA at 1-800-621-3362 or visit a Disaster Recovery Center to inquire about your household's specific options.
